analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the potential of LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from human breast milk, as a passive immunization strategy against respiratory viruses. The research addresses the limitations of current approaches, which rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies. The study demonstrates that LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus, including H5N1. title_zh: 多克隆母乳来源的分泌型 IgA 赋予 抗病毒药物 广泛的针对多种呼吸道病毒的保护作用
source_body_en: Passive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk-derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

title: Rethinking avian influenza control: a systems-oriented One Health perspective for family poultry
abstract: Early detection and control of high- and low-pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI, LPAI) in family poultry flocks remain challenging in settings where mortality from enzootic diseases such as Newcastle disease (ND) and infectious bursal disease (IBD) is persistently high. High background mortality obscures recognition of unusual disease events and delays reporting. In addition to epidemiological constraints, rebuilding trust among family poultry producers, particularly those affected by uncompensated culling during previous HPAI outbreaks, is essential for effective control. Locally grounded, participatory approaches that recognize the lived experience of both women and men poultry keepers are required to strengthen surveillance, reporting, and response. This policy-oriented rapid review synthesized 110 peer-reviewed publications and 27 policy and guidance documents to examine the structural, epidemiological and socio-economic factors influencing HPAI and LPAI prevention and control in family poultry systems. Effective HPAI and LPAI control should be embedded within a broader, systems-oriented strategy that improves overall poultry productivity and explicitly values smallholder knowledge and participation. A multi-hazard risk management approach grounded in One Health is required, i.e., one that addresses equity, food and nutrition security, livelihoods, climate resilience, and global health. Building on a nine-factor assessment of the factors shaping avian influenza control feasibility, we group practical entry points into three complementary themes: (1) structural constraints within family poultry production systems, including the use of locally adapted poultry genotypes, safe, improved access to safe markets and sustainable feed systems, and effective control of enzootic vaccine-preventable diseases; (2) governance, institutional and social barriers, including culturally appropriate outbreak preparedness and response protocols; (3) gender and socio-economic equity, encompassing participatory approaches grounded in inclusivity, transparency, and accountability. Functional cross-sectoral collaboration between public health, animal health, and environmental sectors, along with local government, is essential if One Health approaches are to deliver tangible, cost-effective reductions in zoonotic risk and effective response while supporting sustainable household food and nutrition security.

title: The Risk of an H5N1 Influenza Pandemic
abstract: The last 110 years have seen four influenza A pandemics, where viruses have emerged from mammals or birds with the ability to transmit and cause disease in human populations. Since 2021, a high-pathogenicity strain of avian influenza, H5N1, has caused a panzootic (pandemic of animals), with global spread in wild birds, resulting in frequent spillovers into farmed poultry and into mammals, including mammal species not previously known to be affected by influenza A. This has created increased opportunity for reassortment, mutation, human infection, and potential adaptation to transmit. The risk to humans and the impact are difficult to quantify but of mounting concern to public health bodies. Here, we examine the risk of an H5N1 pandemic emerging and spreading in humans and the potential impact of an H5N1 pandemic.

title: Parental Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Toward Influenza Vaccine Uptake Among Children in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: Seasonal influenza is a major public health concern, particularly among children who are at high risk of infection and can transmit the virus to others. Vaccination is the primary preventive measure. Parental knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) may influence vaccination decisions. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among Saudi parents attending primary healthcare centers in Jeddah. Parents with at least one child aged six months or older were eligible. Data were collected using a validated self-administered Arabic questionnaire assessing knowledge, attitudes, awareness, perceived barriers, and vaccine uptake. title: H9N2 avian influenza virus in Muscovy ducks: a nationwide epidemiological survey and vaccine efficacy assessment
abstract: Abstract Avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are recognized as persistent threats to poultry health and global food security. The H9N2 subtype is widely distributed in poultry. A nationwide epidemiological survey was conducted in South, North, Central, and Southwest China, including Muscovy duck farms and live poultry markets, from 2022 to 2024. A total of 1208 Muscovy duck serum samples, 1212 duck-derived oropharyngeal/cloacal swabs and lung/tracheal tissues, and 480 chicken-derived samples were collected. In addition, 31 H9N2 strains were isolated, 2 of which were duck derived and 29 of which were chicken derived. A novel coinfection challenge model combining ocularnasal inoculation of H9N2 with injection of Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) was established, which induced severe tracheal lesions that closely resembled naturally occurring field pathologies. The coinfection challenge model successfully replicated prevalent field scenarios of viral‒bacterial synergism, resulting in severe lung lesions and a significant increase in viral loads. The results demonstrated that inactivated and live-vector vaccines provided more than 80% protection, with significant reductions in viral shedding and clinical symptoms. This study underscores the urgent need for updated vaccines matching circulating strains and the establishment of a validated framework for evaluating poultry vaccines under real-world coinfection scenarios.

title: A spatial transmission model for evaluating interventions during highly pathogenic avian influenza outbreaks
abstract: During infectious disease outbreaks, epidemiological models can be used to project future outbreak dynamics and to explore scenarios under different control measures. Here, we present the spatially explicit avian influenza transmission model that we developed during the 2026 WiLiMan-ID consortium Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Modelling Challenge, which involved evaluating control measures (preventive and reactive culling, confinement and restocking bans) during a hypothetical avian influenza outbreak. We show that the control measures that were expected to reduce transmission effectively varied between different outbreak stages. For example, policy-makers could choose whether to focus culling efforts on: i) faster reactive culling and no preventive culling; or ii) slower reactive culling and preventive culling. Relatively early in the outbreak, when the number of available culling teams was limited, our results indicate that the two culling strategies were projected to lead to similar numbers of premises with notified infections over the following 28 days. Later in the outbreak, with more culling teams available, the second strategy was projected to lead to substantially fewer notified premises than the first strategy. In addition, we demonstrate that whether a strategy is beneficial or detrimental depends on policy-makers' objectives. For example, preventive culling may reduce transmission, but at the cost of culling poultry on premises without infections, illustrating a trade-off between limiting transmission and the cost of interventions. Our results highlight the importance of choosing policy objectives carefully and reassessing interventions at different outbreak stages to ensure that control policies remain appropriate for the current epidemiological situation.

title: Pathogenesis and Cross-species Potential of Emerging H3N3 Influenza Viruses with Mammalian-adaptive Mutations
abstract: The emergence of triple-reassortant H3N3 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) poses a threat to poultry and public health.This study characterized three novel H3N3 isolates (SQ2049, HN0120, and GT2125) from chickens in China, evaluating their evolution, pathogenicity, and vaccine efficacy.Phylogenetic analysis revealed these isolates originated from H10N3 and H3N8 lineages, carrying an H9N2-derived internal gene backbone.Although identified as low pathogenic AIVs (IVPI=0), they exhibited distinct replicative fitness.GT2125 showed reduced efficiency in embryos, and carried unique PB2 substitutions (V598I and K702).Pathogenicity trials in SPF chickens demonstrated that SQ2049 achieves efficient horizontal transmission in SPF chickens without clinical signs.Notably, cloacal viral shedding persisted for 11 days, whereas oral viral shedding only lasted 2 to 3 day, with mild histopathological lesions observed in the trachea and immune organs.Importantly, the inactivated SQ2049 vaccine elicited high cross-reactive antibody titers (HI≥8log2) and provided 100% protection in SPF chickens.Mouse infection studies identified two HA substitutions (G174E and N209D) after viral replication in mice.These two mutations have previously been associated with mammalian adaptation and enhanced binding to human-type α-2,6 receptors, though their functional effects in the H3N3 context were not evaluated in this study.These findings expand our understanding of H3N3 AIV evolutionary dynamics and highlight the importance of surveillance for reassortant influenza viruses.The demonstrated vaccine efficacy provides a foundation for future H3N3 prevention and control strategies.

title: AEX-1: A Vero cell variant with enhanced permissiveness for influenza virus replication
abstract: BACKGROUND: Continuous cell substrates with improved permissiveness for influenza virus replication are of considerable interest for vaccine development and manufacturing. Vero cells have an excellent regulatory track record; however, their relatively low influenza virus productivity limits their broader application. METHODS: We developed the AEX-1 cell line by co-cultivating Vero cells with chicken embryo amniotic membrane fragments. Cellular morphology, intracellular acidification, influenza virus replication, transcriptomic profile, genetic stability, and tumorigenicity were evaluated. RESULTS: AEX-1 cells displayed distinct morphology and enhanced endosomal/lysosomal acidification compared with parental Vero cells. At 72 h post-infection, a commonly used harvest time for influenza vaccine virus production, AEX-1 cells produced higher infectious titres of WHO-recommended egg-derived A/Sydney/5/2021 (H1N1)pdm09-like and B/Austria/1359417/2021 vaccine viruses, with titres approaching those obtained in embryonated chicken eggs and exceeding Vero cell yields by 0.9-1.7 log10 EID50/ml. No replication advantage was observed for the egg-derived A/Croatia/10136RV/2023 (H3N2) vaccine virus, carrying the egg-adaptive HA G53D substitution, or for the egg-derived A/duck/Vietnam/NCVD-1584/2012 (H5N1) vaccine strain. However, the A/Darwin/9/2021-like Vero-derived primary isolate A/Austria/1516645/2022 (H3N2), lacking G53D, reached infectious titres up to 3.0 log10 TCID50/ml higher than in Vero and 2.3 log10 TCID50/ml higher than in MDCK cells. H1N1 UniFluVec-based influenza virus vectors also replicated efficiently in AEX-1 cells. Transcriptomic analysis revealed changes in genes involved in proton transport, vesicular acidification, and intracellular pH regulation. AEX-1 remained genetically stable after prolonged passaging and showed no evidence of increased tumorigenicity in vitro or in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: Enhanced intracellular acidification may contribute to improved influenza virus replication in AEX-1 cells, suggesting that modulation of endosomal acidification may provide a rational strategy for developing improved cell substrates for influenza vaccine production.

title: Identifying the immunocompetence markers at weaning to predict long-term vaccine response and persistence in pigs
abstract: Vaccination is a key strategy for controlling infectious disease in pigs, but the magnitude and persistence of vaccine-induced immunity vary among individuals. We investigated whether immune and physiological traits measured at weaning could predict long-term antibody (Ab) status and Ab persistence following vaccination against Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (MH) and Influenza A virus (IAV), and whether predictive markers were shared between vaccines. Two vaccination trials were conducted in a cohort of 381 Large White pigs (MH, n=189; IAV, n=192). Animals were vaccinated at weaning (28 days of age) and received a booster 21 days later. Long-term Ab status was defined at 118 days post-vaccination (dpv) using assay-specific thresholds, while Ab persistence was defined as the decline from the individual peak response at 28 or 35 dpv to 118 dpv. A broad panel of immune and physiological traits measured at weaning was evaluated as candidate predictors. Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (sPLS-DA) was used for variable selection, followed by PLS-DA classification models. Cross-validated accuracies ranged from 64.7% to 67.7%, indicating moderate predictive performance. Across vaccines, eight predictors were shared for long-term Ab status and twelve for Ab persistence. Hematocrit, IgG, platelet count, and plateletcrit (PCT) were associated with positive long-term Ab status for both vaccines, whereas mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) and neutrophil percentage were associated with negative status. For persistence, higher vitamin D, -1 globulin concentration, platelet count, and PCT were consistently associated with persistent responses across vaccines, while MCHC and spectral absorbance traits were associated with non-persistence. These findings indicate that early-life immune and physiological traits measured at weaning are associated with immunocompetence traits that contribute to variation in subsequent long-term vaccine antibody outcomes and responsiveness. The identification of both shared and vaccine- or phenotype-specific predictors suggests that vaccine responsiveness reflects both general features of baseline immunocompetence and context-specific determinants.

We investigated whether immune and physiological traits measured at weaning could predict long-term antibody (Ab) status and Ab persistence following vaccination against Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (MH) and Influenza A virus (IAV), and whether predictive markers were shared between vaccines. Two vaccination trials were conducted in a cohort of 381 Large White pigs (MH, n=189; IAV, n=192). Animals were vaccinated at weaning (28 days of age) and received a booster 21 days later. Long-term Ab status was defined at 118 days post-vaccination (dpv) using assay-specific thresholds, while Ab persistence was defined as the decline from the individual peak response at 28 or 35 dpv to 118 dpv. A broad panel of immune and physiological traits measured at weaning was evaluated as candidate predictors. Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (sPLS-DA) was used for variable selection, followed by PLS-DA classification models. Cross-validated accuracies ranged from 64.7% to 67.7%, indicating moderate predictive performance. Across vaccines, eight predictors were shared for long-term Ab status and twelve for Ab persistence. Hematocrit, IgG, platelet count, and plateletcrit (PCT) were associated with positive long-term Ab status for both vaccines, whereas mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) and neutrophil percentage were associated with negative status. For persistence, higher vitamin D, -1 globulin concentration, platelet count, and PCT were consistently associated with persistent responses across vaccines, while MCHC and spectral absorbance traits were associated with non-persistence. These findings indicate that early-life immune and physiological traits measured at weaning are associated with immunocompetence traits that contribute to variation in subsequent long-term vaccine antibody outcomes and responsiveness. The identification of both shared and vaccine- or phenotype-specific predictors suggests that vaccine responsiveness reflects both general features of baseline immunocompetence and context-specific determinants.

title: A prospective, comparative cohort analysis of influenza antibody waning in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation
abstract: Background: Reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic prompted concern about waning of population immunity that could lead to subsequent surges in circulation. We compared longitudinal influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong, two regions with reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods: In two prospective cohort studies (HIVE, Michigan; EPI-HK, Hong Kong), we analyzed longitudinal serum samples collected from 2020 through 2023 from participants without influenza infection or vaccination. Sera were tested using hemagglutination inhibition assays (HAI) and microneutralization (MN) against vaccine strains. Two-year fold changes in titers were estimated using multivariable power-law models adjusted for age and baseline titer. Results: We analyzed 173 sera from 57 HIVE participants and 259 sera from 60 EPI-HK participants. Initial HAI geometric mean titers ranged from 12.3-123.4 in HIVE and 6.3-40.9 in EPI-HK. Among those with >1:40 baseline titers in HIVE, fold-change estimates indicated waning for H1N1 strains, including A/Brisbane (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86]), A/Idaho (0.40 [0.32,0.50]), and A/Michigan (0.43 [0.34,0.52]), while H3N2 and influenza B showed minimal or no waning. In EPI-HK, fold-change estimates demonstrated heterogeneous patterns by strain for H1N1, and waning for selected H3N2 strains, including A/Cambodia (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) and A/Singapore (0.48 [0.33,0.69]). MN results were consistent with HAI findings. Conclusion: Influenza antibody responses during the pandemic showed heterogeneous, strain-specific changes rather than uniform decline. These findings suggest that population immunity was maintained for many strains despite reduced viral circulation, with waning occurring in particular strains and varying by population.

title: Myeloid cell expression of the VDR and parathyroid hormone control the host response to influenza infection in mice

source_records.title: Myeloid cell expression of the VDR and parathyroid hormone control the host response to influenza infection in mice

full_text: IntroductionRespiratory infections caused by seasonal influenza viruses remain a major global health burden. Vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling regulates immune responses, but the role of the VDR and its interaction with parathyroid hormone (PTH) in host resistance to H1N1 influenza infection is not understood.MethodsGlobal VDR knockout (KO) mice, or myeloid (M) deletion of the VDR (M-VDR KO) and the respective wildtype (WT) littermates were infected with H1N1 influenza virus. Additional experiments treated WT mice with intermittent PTH or vehicle and then infected them with a H1N1 influenza A virus. Disease severity, mortality, viral burden and clearance, lung pathology, and inflammatory cytokine responses were evaluated.ResultsH1N1 influenza infection of WT mice resulted in non-lethal disease, whereas VDR KO mice had 21% mortality, delayed viral clearance, more severe symptoms and lung pathology. The increased severity of respiratory disease was accompanied by higher type I and II interferon responses in the lungs. M-VDR KO mice had increased disease severity and delayed viral clearance compared to WT littermates. PTH-treated WT mice had increased clinical scores, influenza M gene, and cytokine responses compared to vehicle treated WT mice.DiscussionThe work describes a novel paradigm in which the vitamin D-PTH axis governs host resistance to influenza virus disease by controlling the amount of inflammation and the amount of virus in the lung. In addition, the data suggest that VDR expression in myeloid cells is critical for controlling the early innate immune response to influenza viruses. Graphical abstract Diagram illustrating H1N1 influenza virus infection in mice, comparing normal and vitamin D receptor knockout (VDR KO) responses. Vitamin D signaling via VDR leads to resolution of infection, while absence of VDR results in hyper-inflammation, elevated IFNβ and IFNγ, and worsened lung pathology. Materials and methodsMiceC57BL/6 VDR KO (VDRCre+/+, KO) and (VDRCre-/-) WT littermates were used for experiments as previously described (20). full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionRespiratory infections caused by seasonal influenza viruses remain a major global health burden. Vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling regulates immune responses, but the role of the VDR and its interaction with parathyroid hormone (PTH) in host resistance to H1N1 influenza infection is not understood.MethodsGlobal VDR knockout (KO) mice, or myeloid (M) deletion of the VDR (M-VDR KO) and the respective wildtype (WT) littermates were infected with H1N1 influenza virus. Additional experiments treated WT mice with intermittent PTH or vehicle and then infected them with a H1N1 influenza A virus. Disease severity, mortality, viral burden and clearance, lung pathology, and inflammatory cytokine responses were evaluated.ResultsH1N1 influenza infection of WT mice resulted in non-lethal disease, whereas VDR KO mice had 21% mortality, delayed viral clearance, more severe symptoms and lung pathology. The increased severity of respiratory disease was accompanied by higher type I and II interferon responses in the lungs. M-VDR KO mice had increased disease severity and delayed viral clearance compared to WT littermates. PTH-treated WT mice had increased clinical scores, influenza M gene, and cytokine responses compared to vehicle treated WT mice.DiscussionThe work describes a novel paradigm in which the vitamin D-PTH axis governs host resistance to influenza virus disease by controlling the amount of inflammation and the amount of virus in the lung. In addition, the data suggest that VDR expression in myeloid cells is critical for controlling the early innate immune response to influenza viruses. Graphical abstract Diagram illustrating H1N1 influenza virus infection in mice, comparing normal and vitamin D receptor knockout (VDR KO) responses. Vitamin D signaling via VDR leads to resolution of infection, while absence of VDR results in hyper-inflammation, elevated IFNβ and IFNγ, and worsened lung pathology.

full_text_sections.results: ResultsVDR KO mice develop lethal H1N1 influenza virus infectionTo determine the role of the VDR in host resistance to influenza virus infection, WT and VDR KO mice were infected with 30 TCID50 H1N1 influenza virus. At this dose of H1N1 influenza virus, none of the 36 WT mice reached endpoint criteria (Figure 1A). Conversely, VDR KO mice had 79% survival rates (n=22 of 28 survived to d14), which were significantly less than the survival of WT mice (Figure 1A). Both WT and VDR KO mice lost about 10% of their starting body weight and body weight loss peaked at d8 post-infection with the surviving mice recovering their body weight by d12 post-infection (Figure 1B). VDR KO mice infected with 30 TCID50 H1N1 virus had 8.3% decrease in gastrocnemius muscle mass at d9 post-infection (Supplementary Figure 2B), however, the muscle wasting was not seen in WT mice infected with 30 TCID50 H1N1 virus. There was no difference between WT and VDR KO gastrocnemius muscle mass at baseline. Respiratory distress and lethargy scores started earlier post-infection (d3) and were significantly more severe in VDR KO than WT mice (Figures 1C, D, p < 0.0001). Influenza viral M gene expression was detected in the lung from d3-d9 post-infection and M gene expression was significantly higher in VDR KO lung than WT lung (Figure 2A; d3 and d9, p < 0.05). TCID50 assays for infectious H1N1 influenza virus confirmed the higher titers of virus in the VDR KO mouse lungs compared to WT mouse lungs at d6 post-infection (Figure 2B; p < 0.01). Histopathology showed that the WT mouse lungs had less perivascular and alveolar inflammation than VDR KO mouse lungs at d9 post-infection, resulting in total pathology scores that were significantly higher for VDR KO than WT mouse lungs (Figures 2C–E, p < 0.05). Collectively, the data show that VDR KO mice are more susceptible to H1N1 influenza virus disease than their WT littermates.Figure 1VDR KO exacerbates disease severity following influenza virus infection. WT and VDR KO mice were infected intranasally with H1N1 influenza virus and monitored over a 14-day period. (A) Kaplan–Meier survival curves, (B) body weight change, (C) respiratory scores, and (D) lethargy scores were recorded daily post-infection. Values are the mean ± SEM and represent pooled results from two to three independent experiments (WT: n = 36; VDR KO: n = 28 total). Statistical significance was determined using the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test for survival (A) and two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test adjusted using the two-stage step-up Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli false discovery rate (FDR) procedure for (B–D). *p < 0.05; ****p < 0.0001.Four-panel figure comparing WT and VDR KO groups post-infection: panel A shows higher survival in WT than VDR KO; panel B shows percent weight change with similar trends in both groups; panels C and D show that VDR KO mice have higher respiratory and lethargy scores, with statistical significance indicated.Figure 2Increased viral burden and pathology in VDR KO mice. Lungs from influenza virus infected WT and VDR KO mice. (A) Influenza viral matrix (M) gene expression (n = 3 for (d0), n=7 mice/all other time points, 3 experiments), (B) viral titers (log10 TCID50/g lung tissue) on d6 post-infection (n=5 per group, 1 experiment), (C) Representative images are shown from lungs from WT and VDR KO mice at d9 post-infection, with the lowest (top row) and highest (bottom row) inflammation scores within each genotype (n = 5–6 mice/group, 2 experiments). Pathologic features are labeled as follows: (a) lymphocyte infiltration, (b) perivascular and peribronchiolar cuffing, and (c) alveolar hemorrhage. Images taken at 40X magnification; scale bars = 100 μm, (D) histopathological scoring (scale 0-3), and (E) quantification of total lung pathology scores (scale 0-9). Values are the mean ± SEM from one to three independent experiments. Each symbol represents an individual mouse. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test for A, and unpaired Student’s t-tests for (B–D) *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01.Panel A shows a line graph comparing M gene fold expression over time post-infection in wild-type (WT) and VDR knockout (VDR KO) groups, with VDR KO displaying higher expression at days three and nine. Panel B provides a dot plot indicating significantly higher virus titers in VDR KO than WT. Panel C presents lung tissue histology images comparing WT and VDR KO, with VDR KO exhibiting more pronounced lymphocyte infiltration, perivascular infiltration, and alveolar hemorrhage. Panel D displays bar graphs quantifying these histopathological features, with significant differences in alveolar hemorrhagic lesions. Panel E shows higher total histopathological scores in VDR KO compared to WT.Overproduction of cytokines in the VDR KO lung following H1N1 infectionUninfected (d0), lungs from WT and VDR KO mice expressed very low levels of Ddx58 (viral RNA sensor, RIG-I), Nfkb1, Ifn-β, Il-6, Il-17a, Ifn-γ, and Il-10 mRNA (Figure 3). In contrast, uninfected VDR KO lungs had high expression of Tnf-α, indicating an increased inflammatory tone prior to infection (Figure 3D, p < 0.001). Ddx58 expression was induced following H1N1 infection in both WT and VDR KO lungs, with VDR KO mice having significantly higher expression at d6 and d9 post-infection compared with WT mice (Figure 3A, p < 0.05). Similarly, Nfkb1 transcript levels were significantly higher in VDR KO lungs at d6 and d9 (Figure 3B, p < 0.01). Peak cytokine responses were at d3 for Ifn-β, Il-6, Il-17a and Tnf-α or d6 for Ifn-γ and Il-10 (Figure 3). Ifn-β mRNA levels were significantly higher (10-fold more) in VDR KO compared to WT lungs at d3 post-infection (Figure 3C, p < 0.0001). Ifn-β resolved to baseline values by d9 post-infection in WT and in the surviving VDR KO mice (Figure 3C). Infection induced Tnf-α expression in WT lungs, whereas Tnf-α transcript levels in VDR KO lungs remained elevated but were not further increased from the uninfected values (Figure 3D). Il-6 mRNA was still detectable in VDR KO mice at d9, while WT resolved to baseline by d9 (not significantly different, Figure 3E). Both VDR KO and WT resolved the Il-6 response by d14 post-infection (Figure 3E). Ifn-γ mRNA peaked at d6 post-infection and resolved back to baseline in both WT and VDR KO mice (Figure 3F). Il-17a mRNA was relatively low in the lung throughout the infection of both WT and VDR KO mice (Figure 3G). Il-10 mRNA expression was induced to the same level in the lungs of WT and VDR KO mice from d3-d9 post-H1N1 infection (Figure 3H). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionVDR KO mice develop severe influenza virus infection characterized by higher viral loads, increased symptoms, more severe histopathology, and muscle wasting compared to WT controls. The increased severity of influenza in VDR KO mice correlates with the robust immune infiltration and dysregulated cytokine expression in the lungs, particularly at d9 post-infection. The increased mortality of the VDR KO mice was not observed in the M-VDR KO mice at the same influenza A virus dose, suggesting that VDR expression in other cells contributes to the mortality of the full VDR KO mice. PTH treatments of WT mice exacerbated influenza disease outcomes. Demonstrating for the first time that vitamin D status and PTH shape antiviral immunity and pulmonary inflammation following influenza virus infection.IFN-β is critical for early viral control and the induction of adaptive immunity (28, 29). Severe influenza virus infection of mice corresponded to high type-I interferons and excessive inflammation (30, 31). RIG-I (Ddx58) and NF-κB (Nfkb1) are central components of the innate immune response to influenza virus, functioning upstream of type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine production. RIG-I serves as a cytosolic sensor of viral RNA and signals through MAVS to activate IRF3/7 and NF-κB, leading to induction of IFN-β and pro-inflammatory mediators (32). VDR KO mice had high Tnf-α expression in the lung before infection that remained high throughout the influenza infection. In addition, lungs from VDR KO mice had significantly higher Ifn-β at d3 and Ddx58 at d6 and d9 post-infection than WT littermates. VDR expression is needed to control the amplitude of the early innate viral sensing and downstream inflammatory response to influenza in the lung.The increased susceptibility of the M-VDR KO mice to influenza, further supports the importance of myeloid cells as vitamin D targets that control the innate and acquired immune response to influenza. Myeloid cell-intrinsic VDR signaling is required for proper regulation of innate antiviral responses and efficient viral clearance. Myeloid cells, including macrophages and inflammatory antigen-presenting cells, are among the first immune cells to recognize influenza virus through pattern recognition receptors such as RIG-I and initiate antiviral cytokine production. Vitamin D has been shown to inhibit NF-κB dependent transcription and limit inflammation (33). Heightened RIG-I and NF-κB associated responses in VDR KO mice contribute to the increased type I interferon response observed early after influenza infection.Cytokine storms are often the cause of secondary bacterial infections and hospitalization for humans with severe influenza infections (31, 34). The cytokine storms that include IL-17A, TNF-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ etc. play a complex role in viral infections, promoting neutrophil recruitment, anti-viral immunity and cytotoxic T cells but also contributing to lung damage (35, 36). Vitamin D has been shown to decrease IFN-γ and to inhibit the differentiation and proliferation of Th1 cells (37). VDR KO lungs had higher numbers of IFN-γ secreting cells compared to WT lungs following influenza infection. Blocking IFN-γ signaling using anti-IFN-γ therapy significantly alleviated acute lung injury in mice infected with H1N1 influenza virus, demonstrating that excessive IFN-γ contributes to immunopathology (38). VDR KO lungs had higher IL-10 production at d14 post-infection than WT lungs. IL-10 is a key immunoregulatory cytokine that limits inflammation and tissue damage (39). Experimentally, IFN-β treatments have been shown to induce IL-10 secreting Tregs and therefore the increased IL-10 late post-infection could be connected to the high IFN-β at d3 post-infection (40). High Il-17a, Tnf-α, Ifn-β, Ifn-γ and Il-10 mRNA expression with more IFN-γ secreting T cells in the VDR KO lungs corresponded with the increased severity of H1N1 influenza symptoms compared to lungs from WT mice. Cytokine dysregulation is a feature of VDR KO mice.Vitamin D deficiency and VDR KO result in high PTH levels. PTH treatments of WT mice resulted in the increased severity of influenza virus, higher viral M gene and IFN-γ compared to vehicle-treated WT mice. PTH receptors have been demonstrated to be on T cells, and PTH has been shown to induce IL-17A production (19). Patients with chronic kidney disease and hyperparathyroidism have immune dysregulation that results in higher risks of infection (41). CD25 is the alpha chain of the IL-2 receptor and has been shown to be expressed late following activation on conventional T cells and constitutively on regulatory T cells (42). FoxP3 has also been shown to be expressed transiently in activated conventional T cells and stably in Tregs (43). In vitro PTH and 1,25(OH)2D both induced CD25+ expression on CD4+ T cells and in vivo PTH treatments increased FoxP3+ expressing Tregs. Together the results are consistent with the literature that shows that intermittent PTH expands Tregs in humans and mice (44) and the extensive literature that shows that 1,25(OH)2D and vitamin D status support both CD4CD25+ and FoxP3+ expressing regulatory T cells (45–50). The effect of VDR KO to increase IL-10 and PTH to induce Tregs, while many inflammatory cytokines are over produced, may seem paradoxical. Perhaps the timing of Treg/IL-10 response is too late to stop the inflammation leading to severe disease in VDR KO mice. IFN-γ is a key antiviral cytokine but also a potent driver of pulmonary inflammation and tissue injury following influenza infection (51, 52). These findings suggest that loss of VDR signaling or elevated PTH shifts the immune response toward exaggerated IFN-γ–mediated inflammation, eliciting a compensatory but delayed regulatory response. It is possible that the daily repeated PTH administration does not adequately model the chronic high PTH levels in VDR KO mice. The daily repeated PTH administrations did not alter serum calcium levels, excluding calcium signaling as a major contributor to influenza severity and demonstrating that intermittent PTH itself contributes to worsened disease outcomes during influenza infection. The finding that intermittent PTH contributes to immune dysfunction, resulting in a severe form of H1N1 influenza virus infection is a novel finding.There are several limitations to the current study. First, intermittent PTH treatment of WT mice does not fully replicate the chronic PTH elevation observed in VDR KO mice. While osmotic pumps delivering continuous PTH could have been used to mimic chronic elevation, doing so would likely have disrupted mineral homeostasis and induce additional physiological confounders. Nevertheless, the current data still support a distinct effect of intermittent PTH on the host response to influenza. Second, the data supporting the overproduction of cytokines in response to PTH treatment and VDR deletion remain kinetic and correlative. To establish a causal link for the elevated levels of IFN-β1 and IFN-γ, additional experiments utilizing neutralizing antibodies or knockout models are required. However, given the extensive existing literature connecting both the VDR and PTH to increased inflammatory tone, our data strongly support the claims of heightened cytokine production in VDR KO and PTH-treated mice. Third, the influenza M gene was utilized as a surrogate for viral quantification in these experiments. Fortunately, the day 6 data in Figure 3—showing that VDR KO mice had both higher M gene expression and a higher load of infectious viral titers (TCID50) than WT mice—supports a true difference in viral clearance. Lastly, myeloid cells are highly heterogeneous, and confirming VDR depletion in BMDM does not definitively prove deletion within lung myeloid cells. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSeasonal and pandemic influenza viruses continue to pose significant global health challenges, contributing to millions of cases of severe respiratory illness and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year (1). Although vaccines and antiviral medications are available, their efficacy varies by strain and season. Disease severity during influenza virus infection is determined not only by viral pathogenicity, but also by the magnitude and regulation of host immune responses. While early innate antiviral signaling and interferon production are essential for viral clearance, excessive or prolonged inflammation can result in lung injury, impaired viral resolution, and severe disease (2). Identifying host pathways that balance protective versus pathogenic antiviral immunity is therefore critical for understanding susceptibility to severe influenza virus infection.Vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent worldwide and has been associated with increased susceptibility to respiratory infections, including influenza virus infection (3). Observational studies have demonstrated inverse correlations between circulating serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and incidence of upper respiratory tract infections in both children and adults (4, 5). Furthermore, a large meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials demonstrated that vitamin D supplementation significantly reduced the risk of acute respiratory infections, particularly in individuals with profound vitamin D deficiency (6). However, clinical studies examining vitamin D supplementation during viral respiratory infections have produced inconsistent results, suggesting that the mechanisms by which vitamin D regulates antiviral immunity remain incompletely understood (7).The biological effects of vitamin D are mediated through the vitamin D receptor (VDR), a nuclear receptor expressed in epithelial cells and multiple immune cell populations, including macrophages, dendritic cells, and activated T lymphocytes (8). The effect of VDR KO on host resistance to infection has been studied for bacterial and parasitic infections, but not viruses (9–12). Immune cells from VDR KO mice have been shown to overproduce inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-β1, IL-1β, IL-12, and IFN-γ that contribute to susceptibility to colitis, infection and autoimmunity (9–12). T cells from VDR KO mice proliferate more quickly and over- produce IFN-γ and IL-17 (9, 10). Because of the critical role of IFN-γ on host resistance to influenza virus by promoting antiviral immunity and viral clearance (11, 12), the effect of high IFN-γ on the host response of VDR KO mice to influenza infection is difficult to predict.There is evidence that vitamin D may be a direct regulator of some viruses. Human bronchial epithelial cells have been shown to produce the vitamin D hydroxylase that produces the high affinity VDR binding compound, 1,25(OH)2D (13). 1,25(OH)2D treatment of human bronchial epithelial cells induced cathelicidin that suppressed respiratory syncytial virus replication in vitro (13). Although respiratory syncytial virus is a common respiratory illness that belongs to a different viral family than influenza virus, there is the possibility of direct effects of vitamin D on host responses that control viral replication.An additional and largely unexplored component of vitamin D biology during infection is its close endocrine relationship with parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH, a calcium-regulating peptide hormone, is secreted in response to low vitamin D status. PTH induces the production of the vitamin D hydroxylase to increase the circulating levels of 1,25(OH)2D (14). In a feedback loop, 1,25(OH)2D production inhibits PTH and together regulates serum calcium and phosphorous levels (14). Vitamin D deficiency and VDR KO result in very high PTH levels (15) even when calcium is normalized by rescue diets (16). PTH has recently been shown to be an immune system regulator (17–19). Importantly, PTH signaling enhanced T cell proliferation, and inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., TNF-α, IL-17) (17–19). Elevated PTH levels may contribute to the enhanced inflammation and cytokine production present in VDR KO mice.VDR KO mice developed more severe and lethal influenza disease, characterized by heightened type I and II interferon production, with delayed viral clearance. Intermittent PTH treatment of WT mice exacerbated respiratory signs of influenza virus infection and resulted in higher viral M gene expression compared to vehicle-treated WT mice. PTH treated WT mice had greater IFN-γ production, elevated viral M gene and more severe clinical signs. Influenza infection of myeloid (M) specific, M-VDR KO mice, had impaired anti-viral responses and increased severity of symptoms. The increased susceptibility of the M-VDR KO mice demonstrates a critical role for myeloid cells as vitamin D targets in the host response to influenza. The combined effects of VDR KO and high PTH (16) result in excessive cytokine responses that are ineffective for host resistance to influenza viruses. Instead, the increased inflammation adds to the tissue injury. Interventions with vitamin D, would increase vitamin D status and reduce PTH, that potentially could reduce the impact of influenza virus infection. MiceC57BL/6 VDR KO (VDRCre+/+, KO) and (VDRCre-/-) WT littermates were used for experiments as previously described (20). For myeloid (M)-specific deletion studies, VDR floxed mice (VDRfl/fl) were crossed with LysM-Cre transgenic mice (B6.129P2-Lyz2tm1(cre)Ifo/J), Jackson Laboratory, stock #004781) to generate M-VDR KO (VDRfl/fl LysMCre+) and WT littermate controls. Genotyping primer sequences and expected PCR product sizes are provided in Supplementary Table S1. Experiments used 8–10 wk old mice of both sexes. There were no significant effects of sex on survival, body weight loss, and lethargy in WT and VDR KO mice and on respiratory symptoms in VDR KO mice following influenza infection (Supplementary Figure 1). There were significantly less respiratory symptoms in WT males late following the influenza infection than WT females (Supplementary Figure 1). Subsequent experiments were not powered to examine sex as a variable which is a limitation of the study. VDR KO and their WT littermates were fed vitamin D containing and high-lactose rescue diets (20% high lactose; Envigo, TD 96348, Madison, WI). All other experiments that used WT mice treated with PTH/vehicle or M-VDR KO and WT littermates used the same vitamin D containing diets but without the high-lactose (Envigo, TD 89124). All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Pennsylvania State University (University Park, PA). title_original: Myeloid cell expression of the VDR and parathyroid hormone control the host response to influenza infection in mice

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of vitamin D receptor (VDR) and parathyroid hormone (PTH) in modulating the host response to influenza infection, particularly focusing on disease severity, mortality, and inflammatory cytokine responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used C57BL/6 VDR knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) littermates to evaluate the effects of VDR and PTH on influenza infection. Mice were infected with H1N1 influenza virus, and their clinical symptoms, weight loss, and respiratory scores were monitored.
analysis.methods: The study involved genotyping using PCR with primers from Supplementary Table S1, serum calcium measurement via a colorimetric assay, RNA concentration and purity assessment using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) for influenza virus M gene quantitation. Infectious virus was measured using the TCID50 assay, and cell viability was assessed with a hemocytometer and trypan blue.
analysis.main_results: VDR KO mice showed 21% mortality, delayed viral clearance, more severe symptoms, and lung pathology compared to WT littermates. PTH treatment increased clinical scores, influenza M gene levels, and cytokine responses in WT mice compared to vehicle-treated controls.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted their findings as evidence of a novel paradigm where the vitamin D-PTH axis regulates host resistance to influenza virus disease by modulating inflammation and viral load in the lungs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that VDR and PTH pathways could be important targets for understanding and potentially modulating host responses to influenza infection, offering insights into inflammation control and viral clearance mechanisms.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of mice as the model organism, which may not fully translate to human influenza infections. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on animal models and the absence of direct human clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of the vitamin D-PTH axis in modulating the host response to influenza infection in mice. It investigates how VDR knockout (KO) and PTH treatments affect disease severity, mortality, and inflammatory cytokine responses. The research finds that VDR KO mice exhibit increased mortality, delayed viral clearance, and more severe symptoms compared to wild-type (WT) littermates. PTH treatment in WT mice enhances clinical scores, viral load, and cytokine responses. The study uses a combination of genetic models, qRT-PCR, and TCID50 assays to assess these effects. The findings suggest a novel mechanism by which the VDR-PTH axis influences host resistance to influenza, potentially offering new insights into inflammation and viral clearance. However, the study is limited to an animal model, which may affect the generalizability of results to human influenza. The evidence is moderate due to the experimental nature and lack of direct human data.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在探讨维生素 D 受体 (VDR) 和甲状旁腺激素 (PTH) 在调节 宿主 对流感感染反应中的作用,特别关注疾病严重程度、宿主 和炎症细胞因子反应。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用 C57BL/6 VDR 敲除 (KO) 和野生型 (WT) 同窝小鼠来评估 VDR 和 PTH 对流感感染的影响。小鼠感染甲型H1N1流感病毒,监测其临床症状、体重减轻和呼吸评分。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究涉及使用补充表 S1 中引物的 PCR 进行基因分型、通过比色测定进行血清钙测量、使用 NanoDrop 分光光度计评估 RNA 浓度和纯度,以及用于流感病毒 M 基因定量的定量 PCR (qRT-PCR)。使用 TCID50 测定法测量感染性病毒,并使用血细胞计数器和台盼蓝评估细胞活力。
analysis_zh.main_results: 与 WT 同窝小鼠相比,VDR KO 小鼠表现出 21% 的 死亡率、病毒清除延迟、更严重的症状和肺部病理。与媒介物处理的对照组相比,PTH 治疗 增加了 WT 小鼠的临床评分、流感 M 基因水平和细胞因子反应。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将他们的发现解释为一种新范例的证据,其中维生素 D-PTH 轴通过调节肺部炎症和病毒载量来调节 宿主 对流感病毒疾病的抵抗力。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,VDR 和 PTH 通路可能是理解和潜在调节 宿主 对流感感染反应的重要靶点,为炎症控制和病毒清除机制提供见解。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于它使用小鼠作为模型生物,这可能无法完全转化为人类流感感染。由于依赖动物模型且缺乏直接的人体临床数据,证据强度中等。

The study contributes to the understanding of influenza's impact on neurological health in vulnerable populations, but its evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope and absence of comparative data.

title: Seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in Lebanese hospitals: determinants of uptake post-COVID-19 pandemic and economic crisis
abstract: Background Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at increased risk of acquiring and transmitting influenza. We assessed self-reported influenza vaccination uptake among surveyed HCWs in Lebanese hospitals during 2023–2024, compared it with their reported uptake in pre-pandemic 2018–2019, and identified factors associated with non-vaccination. Methods This cross-sectional survey was conducted from April to July 2024 among HCWs from 14 public and private hospitals across multiple regions of Lebanon. The questionnaire assessed influenza vaccination status, free institutional vaccine provision, awareness, attitudes, and COVID-19 vaccine–related perceptions. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with non-vaccination in 2023–2024. Results Among 391 participants, self-reported influenza vaccination uptake was lower in 2023–2024 than in 2018–2019 (29.9% vs 60.5%, p < 0.0001). Free institutional vaccine provision was also lower (39.6% vs 70.1%, p < 0.0001), and 19.2% were willing to pay out of pocket. Higher odds of non-vaccination were observed among HCWs aged <30 years (aOR 3.80, 95% CI 1.96–7.68), non-physicians (aOR 5.17, 95% CI 2.26–12.42), those without free institutional vaccine provision (aOR 17.74, 95% CI 9.38–35.72), those with unfavorable influenza vaccination attitudes (aOR 4.61, 95% CI 2.10–10.63), and those with moderate-to-high COVID-19 vaccine–related hesitancy (aOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.03–4.27). Conclusion Among surveyed HCWs, influenza vaccination uptake in 2023–2024 was substantially lower than reported for 2018–2019. Lack of free institutional vaccine provision and unfavorable vaccine-related perceptions were independently associated with non-vaccination. Restoring free workplace-based vaccination and addressing COVID-19 vaccine–related hesitancy may improve uptake in resource-constrained healthcare settings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估 2023 年至 2024 年黎巴嫩医院医护人员 (HCW) 自我报告的流感 疫苗接种 感染情况,与大流行前的 2018-2019 年感染情况进行比较,并确定与非 疫苗接种 相关的因素。医护人员感染和传播流感的风险增加。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 2024 年 4 月至 7 月,对黎巴嫩多个地区 14 家公立和私立医院的医护人员进行了一项横断面调查。
elements_zh.methods: 该调查评估了流感 疫苗接种 状况、免费机构 疫苗 提供、意识、态度以及与 COVID-19 疫苗 相关的看法。多变量逻辑回归确定了 2023-2024 年与非 疫苗接种 独立相关的因素。
elements_zh.main_results: 在 391 名参与者中,2023-2024 年自我报告的流感 疫苗接种 摄入量低于 2018-2019 年(29.9% vs 60.5%,p < 0.0001)。免费机构 疫苗 拨款也较低(39.6% vs 70.1%,p < 0.0001),19.2% 愿意自付费用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 在年龄 <30 岁的医护人员、非医生、没有免费机构 疫苗 服务的人员、对流感 疫苗接种 态度不利的人员以及对 COVID-19 疫苗 相关犹豫中度至高度的人员中,观察到非 疫苗接种 的几率较高。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 恢复基于工作场所的免费 疫苗接种 并解决与 COVID-19 疫苗 相关的犹豫可能会提高资源有限的医疗保健环境中的使用率。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到横断面设计的限制,无法确定因果关系,并且可能存在自我报告偏差。样本量和区域多样性可能会影响普遍性。

full_text: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies. MATERIALS AND METHODSCells and virusesMadin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), no. CRL-2936] were maintained in minimal essential medium (MEM) (Gibco, 11095080) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16000-044). Human embryonic kidney–293T (HEK-293T) cells (ATCC, no. CRL-3216) were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco, 11965092) supplemented with 10% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16000-044). Both cell types were incubated at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator.The HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 isolate A/Canada Goose/ON/2025, referred to here as genotype D1.1 virus, was obtained from National Centre for Foreign Animal Disease, Canada. The HPAI H5N1 B3.13 genotype isolate A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, referred to here as genotype B3.13 virus, was obtained from the US Department of Agriculture. Both viruses were propagated at a multiplicity of infection of 0.001 on MDCK cells until complete cytopathic effects (CPEs) were observed. Viral growth medium consisted of MEM supplemented with 0.2% bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich, A7030) with l-[(toluene-4-sulphonamido)-2-phenyl] ethyl chloromethyl ketone (1 μg/ml)–trypsin.Generation of vaccine virus by reverse geneticsThe sequences encoding HA and NA genes from the B3.13 H5N1 virus were cloned individually into pHW2000 plasmids. The multiple basic amino acids in the HA protein cleavage site were removed. The HA and NA plasmids, together with the six plasmids representing the rest of the gene segments from A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8), were cotransfected into HEK-293T and MDCK cells to rescue the PR8 + B3.13 (6 + 2) virus (vaccine virus) using reverse genetics (37). Three days posttransfection, supernatant was harvested and used to inoculate 11-day-old embryonated chicken eggs, obtained from the University of Saskatchewan Poultry Teaching and Research Unit. At 3 DPI, allantoic fluid was harvested and inactivated with β-propiolactone at a final concentration of 0.1%, using our validated protocol (38). The inactivated virus was diluted in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Cytiva, SH30256.01) and prepared as a W/O/W vaccine emulsion using, MONTANIDE ISA 201 VG adjuvant (Seppic, Air Liquide Healthcare) following the manufacturer’s directions. One vaccine dose consisted of 1-ml total volume [55% adjuvant:45% antigen in PBS (v/v)] containing 1 × 106 TCID50.Biosafety and ethics statementAll work involving infectious HPAI H5N1 virus was performed in containment level 3 (CL3) laboratories and CL3 large animal facilities at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization (VIDO). Work was completed in compliance with the Canadian Biosafety Standard, third edition, under the authority of the Public Health Agency of Canada and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency. All animal experiments were completed at the University of Saskatchewan following guidelines provided by the Canadian Council on Animal Care and approved by the University Animal Care Committee (protocol no. 20240042).AnimalsTen Alpine dairy goats were sourced from a farm in Saskatchewan, Canada, and housed at the CL3 large animal facility at VIDO. Goats were fed an ad libitum diet consisting of alfalfa timothy hay cube pelleted ration (dairy ration, 16% protein) and water. Goats, milked once daily, were brought onto a milking stanchion (Sydell Inc.), and visible debris was removed from each teat using a WypAll general-purpose wipe saturated with an iodine-based disinfectant. Teats were manually stripped two to three times to allow milk let-down, followed by an additional wipe with the iodine disinfectant before sample collection. Milk from left and right glands was then manually stripped into individual specimen cups for sampling followed by the use of a portable milking machine to complete milk collection. The collection vessel containing the milk was weighed, and milk weights for each goat were recorded. One milking machine was dedicated to the vaccinated goat cohort and the other to the unvaccinated cohort. Individual claws on the machine were paired with designated teats (i.e., left and right) so that the claw was used on the same teat at every milking. After each daily milking, the machines were disinfected with hot water, detergent then sanitizer (12% sodium hypochlorite diluted to 200 parts per million). Gloves worn by personnel were disinfected with Prevail after handling the inoculated gland.Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculationThree goats were acclimated for 7 days before viral challenge. Age and parity of all goats can be found in table S6. All three goats were inoculated in the right mammary gland with 104 TCID50 of HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 in MEM medium (Fig. 1A). The virus inoculum was back titrated to confirm dose. After milking, 1 ml of the viral inoculum was drawn into a sterile 3-ml syringe fitted with a sterile teat cannula. The teat orifice was disinfected using isopropyl alcohol wipes before infusion. The teat cannula was inserted its full length before depositing the solution into the teat canal. Firm pressure was applied to the base of the teat while the cannula was withdrawn and the teat was massaged upward to facilitate movement of the inoculum into the teat cistern. Before the study was initiated, one goat was preselected to be euthanized at 4 DPI (D4) during the period of peak viral shedding in milk, which had previously been identified in dairy cows (20). The remaining two goats were euthanized at 19 DPI (D19) by intravenous injection with Dorminal (20 ml per 45 kg of body weight; Rafter 8 Products Inc.) after resolution of infectious virus shedding in milk.Study design: Vaccination, B3.13 virus challenge, and rechallengeSeven goats were acclimated for 7 days. At D0 (prime) and D21 (boost), three goats were vaccinated subcutaneously in the neck with inactivated vaccine virus formulated with Montanide ISA 201 VG adjuvant (VACC group, n = 3), or with adjuvant alone (ADJ group, n = 3) (Fig. 4A). Groups were balanced in terms of age and parity of goats (table S6). One goat (goat #4) received neither vaccine nor adjuvant. On D35, all seven goats were challenged with 104 TCID50 of genotype B3.13 virus in the right mammary gland, as described in the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section. Five DPC, at study day 40, goat #4 was euthanized for tissue collection during the period of peak viral shedding in milk. At 28 DPC (D63), all remaining goats were rechallenged with 104 TCID50 of genotype B3.13 virus in the left mammary gland, as described above. The virus inoculum was back titrated to confirm dose. Goats were monitored for 10 days post–secondary challenge and were euthanized at D73, as described in the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section. Ten days was chosen for euthanasia after secondary challenge as it corresponds to the period during which infectious viral shedding was observed in cattle after inoculation with this B3.13 genotype strain, ensuring that any shedding following rechallenge would be captured.Sample collectionGoats were monitored daily by veterinarians or veterinary staff. Rectal temperatures were measured, and goats were clinically scored for respiration, depression, and mastitis (table S7). Foremilk was manually stripped from each gland before milking at regular intervals postinoculation for the quantification of infectious virus and viral RNA. Milk from both glands of each goat was collected together and weighed, and daily milk yield was recorded. Blood, feces, nasal swabs, and oral swabs were collected at regular intervals for quantification of viral RNA, as well as serum for measurement of antibody titers. As feces were completely negative for viral RNA during the genotype D1.1 inoculation study (see the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section), feces were not collected in the B3.13 study (see the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section).Viral load titration by TCID50 assayMDCK cells (2.5 × 104 cells per well) were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator overnight. The following day, whole milk was serially diluted tenfold in MEM and added to the plate in triplicate. The plate was incubated for 1 hour at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator, and, then, the inoculum was replaced with viral growth medium supplemented with antibiotic-antimycotic (Gibco, 15240062). CPE was documented at 48 hours postinfection (hpi), and the TCID50 titer was calculated using the Spearman-Kärber algorithm.RNA extraction and RT-qPCRMilk and blood were diluted 1:4 in PBS. Nasal swabs and oral swabs were placed into 1 ml of MEM with antibiotic-antimycotic upon collection. Swabs were vortexed for 30 s and centrifuged at 1600g for 10 min at 4°C, and, then, the supernatant was collected. Each fluid (140 μl) was then added to 560 μl of Buffer AVL, and, then, RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Kit as per the manufacturer’s directions (QIAGEN, 52904).Tissue was placed in RNAlater (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM7020) upon collection. Tissue or feces were each homogenized in 600 μl of Buffer RLT (QIAGEN, 79216) using a TissueLyser II, set to 30 Hz for 5 min, and then centrifuged at 5000g for 10 min at 4°C. The supernatant was collected, and a volume corresponding to 30 mg of starting tissue or feces was transferred to fresh buffer RLT to a total of 600 μl. RNA was extracted using the QIAGEN RNeasy Mini Kit as directed by the manufacturer (QIAGEN, 74104).Quantification of viral RNA was performed by RT-qPCR using the Luna Universal One-Step RT-qPCR Kit (New England Biolabs, E3005). Reactions were prepared in duplicate with 5 μl of RNA template and a primer probe set targeting the influenza A virus M gene. Forward primer sequence: 5′-GGCCCCCTCAAAGCCGA-3′; reverse primer sequence: 5′-CGTCTACGYTGCAGTCC-3′; probe sequence: 5′ (FAM)-TCACTGGGCACGGTGAGCGT-3′ (MGBNFQ) (IDT) (20). Standard curves were generated by extracting RNA from tissue, blood, or MEM spiked with a known titer of H5N1 virus. Standard curves were generated for each RT-qPCR plate and used to interpolate TCID50 equivalents from Ct values.Preparation of milk and serum for antibody measurementRennet from Mucor miehei (0.15 μg/ml) was added to milk samples and incubated at 37°C for 5 min. Centrifugation of the samples at 1300g for 5 min resulted in three fractions: the top fraction consisting of fat, a soluble whey fraction, and a pellet consisting of curdled milk. The top fat fraction was removed carefully with a pipette, and the soluble fraction was collected. The whey was heat inactivated at 60°C for 30 min before use in virus neutralization assays and ELISAs (39). Serum was heat inactivated at 56°C for 30 min for use in virus neutralization assays and heat-treated at 60°C for 30 min for use in ELISAs.Virus neutralization assayMDCK cells (2.5 × 104 cells per well) were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated overnight in a 5% CO2 incubator set to 37°C. The following day, serum or whey samples in quadruplicate were serially diluted twofold in MEM. Samples were mixed with an equal volume of H5N1 virus diluted to 2 × 103 TCID50/ml. Genotype D1.1 virus was used in the virus neutralization assays for the genotype D1.1 inoculation study described in the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section, and genotype B3.13 virus was used in virus neutralization assays for the genotype B3.13 vaccination and challenge study described in the “Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculation” section. Medium on the MDCK cells was replaced with 100 μl of whey or serum mixed with virus, totaling 100 TCID50 of virus per well. CPE was recorded at 48 hpi, and the VN antibody titer was defined as the highest serum or whey dilution that prevented CPE in at least two of the four wells.IDEXX ELISA and HA ELISAThe IDEXX Influenza A Ab test (Influenza A Ab, IDEXX) was conducted per the manufacturer’s guidelines using serum or whey starting at a dilution of 1:10. A sample-to-positive ratio of <0.6 was defined as positive.Soluble HA from A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024 (genotype B3.13) was expressed in HEK-293T cells and purified as previously described (40). The HA coding sequence was cloned into episomal expression vector pEB4.3 (accession no. MG182339). The polybasic cleavage site between HA1 and HA2 (RERRK) was replaced with a threonine residue to prevent cleavage during protein expression.Immulon 2HB 96-well microtiter plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 3655) were coated with HA protein (2 μg/ml) diluted in sodium carbonate buffer (pH 9.6) and incubated overnight at 4°C. Plates were washed with tris-buffered saline (TBS) supplemented with 0.05% v/v Tween 20 (TBS-T) and blocked with 0.1% gelatin from porcine skin (Sigma-Aldrich, G2625) in TBS-T for 1 hour at room temperature (RT). Fourfold serial dilutions of serum (starting at 1:100) or milk (starting at 1:10) in TBS-T and 0.1% gelatin from porcine skin were added to duplicate wells and incubated at RT for 1 hour. For detection of IgG antibodies, Reserve-AP–labeled, rabbit anti-goat IgG (1:10,000 in diluent; KPL catalog no. 5220−0384) was added to each well and incubated for 1 hour at RT. Each well was reacted with 100 μl of p-nitrophenyl phosphate (Sigma-Aldrich, catalog no. N3254) diluted in diethanolamine buffer at a concentration of 1 mg/ml. Reactions were allowed to develop until positive samples reached an absorbance of greater than 2.0 measured at 405 nm, with a reference at 490 nm, using a SpectraMax Plus 384 Reader (Molecular Devices). Antibody titers were determined using the reciprocal of the highest dilution that resulted in an absorbance value greater than the means + 3 SDs of the absorbance value from preimmune samples.Histology and immunohistochemistryTissue samples were immediately submerged in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 7 days and transferred to fresh 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 hours before transfer out of the CL3 laboratory (20). Tissue embedding, sectioning, and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed by Prairie Diagnostic Services and images acquired using an Olympus Virtual Slide Scanning Microscope (Olympus-Life Science) completed by the WCVM Imaging Centre (University of Saskatchewan).Data presentation and statistical analysisGraphPad Prism 11 was used for data visualization. Images were created using BioRender.com. Daily milk yield data were analyzed both within individual phases (postprime, postboost, and postchallenge) and across phases by averaging daily milk yield per goat within each phase. Generalized linear mixed models (GLIMMIX; SAS v9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) were used for all milk yield analyses. Milk yield was modeled as a repeated measure on goat, applying a first-order autoregressive covariance structure, which yielded the lowest Akaike information criterion corrected (AICc). Fixed effects included treatment (VACC versus ADJ), time (day or phase), and their interaction. Denominator degrees of freedom for tests of fixed effects were adjusted using the Kenward-Roger correction, and a Newton-Raphson optimization algorithm with ridging was requested using the NLOPTIONS statement. Multiple means comparisons were adjusted using the Tukey-Kramer method. Variance attributed to individual goats was captured by the repeated measures term; therefore, the random effect of goat was removed from the model. Normality of studentized residuals was visually assessed to confirm model assumptions. Milk yield recorded on the day before primary vaccination (D0) did not differ among treatments (P = 0.76); however, it was included as a covariate in both models (P < 0.01). Parity was evaluated but excluded as it neither improved model fit according to AICc nor altered interpretation of results. Significance was declared when P ≤ 0.05.
