full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONHPAI H5N1 has emerged as a novel mammary infection in dairy cows. The physical size of these animals is a major barrier for many laboratories to conduct HPAI research. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that dairy goats represent a relevant model for HPAI H5N1 mammary infection, given their susceptibility to both D1.1 and B3.13 genotypes and their recapitulation of clinical and virological features similar to those observed in dairy cows (13, 19, 20). Field reports indicate that genotype D1.1 infection in dairy cows causes milder or subclinical disease compared with genotype B3.13 (32). Our preliminary observations suggest that this might be similar in dairy goats. Genotype D1.1 infection resulted in less severe mastitis, a smaller impact on milk yield, no observable changes in milk quality, and a more pronounced rebound in milk production (Fig. 1). The genotype D1.1 virus used in this study was isolated from Canada goose and has avian associated PB2 signatures 627E and 701D but lacks the mammalian-adaptive PB2 M631L substitution that is present in the genotype B3.13 bovine H5N1 isolate. Despite these genetic differences, viral shedding in milk was comparable between the genotypes, indicating that disease severity was influenced by factors beyond viral replication. This likely includes differences in other viral proteins that are known to contribute to pathogenicity, such as NS1, PB1-F2, and PA-X (33–35). Viremia was not evident for either genotype, although low levels of viral RNA were sporadically detected in blood. Genotype D1.1 remained localized to the inoculated right mammary gland with the one goat sacrificed at 4 DPI (D4), revealing that there was minimal spread to extramammary tissues and lymph nodes; by contrast, genotype B3.13 infection was associated with high viral RNA levels in multiple extramammary tissues in the one goat sacrificed at 5 DPC (D5) (table S1 and Fig. 3C). These observations are based on one animal per genotype at a single time point, warranting further validation to determine whether dissemination dynamics is a unique feature for these genotypes. Generally, dissemination of the virus to uninoculated mammary glands is rare in experimental intramammary H5N1 infection of cows, which is similarly observed in all goats, with exception of one goat in which genotype B3.13 infection was detected in both the inoculated and uninoculated mammary gland (Fig. 3, D and E) (19–21). Although the exact cause is unclear, possible explanations include exposure during animal handling, contamination during milking, or virus dissemination within the goat. This model facilitates HPAI H5N1 pathogenesis research in the mammary gland and offers a platform to investigate emerging and existing HPAI H5Nx strains of both avian and mammalian origin.Parenteral administration of the inactivated virus formulated with Montanide ISA 201 adjuvant had no negative effect on milk production in dairy goats. Overall, the vaccine conferred partial protection by reducing the severity of clinical mastitis and significantly limiting milk production losses following challenge (Fig. 5, A, B, and D). Immunization reduced the onset, duration, and amount of infectious virus shedding in milk when compared with the adjuvant alone group (Fig. 5F). We noted a discordance in infectious virus titers and viral RNA in milk of VACC goats, but not ADJ goats (Fig. 5, E and F). Viral titers converted from viral RNA levels were greater than infectious virus recovered in the VACC goats (Fig. 5, E and F), suggesting that H5N1 was replicating in the tissue, but either was subsequently bound by neutralizing antibodies in milk or that immune-mediated clearance of infected cells resulted in shedding of viral debris, including nucleic acids, into milk. Immunization induced VN and NP-specific antibodies as well as H5-specific IgG antibodies, although VN and NP-specific antibodies were undetectable in milk before challenge (Fig. 4). After challenge, VN titers were similar in right and left gland milk of VACC goats, whereas ADJ goats had lower titers in the uninoculated left gland milk compared with right gland milk (Fig. 4, D and E). Together, these data indicate that vaccination was safe and primed immune responses that mitigated clinical disease but did not confer sterilizing immunity. Our vaccine virus contained the hemagglutinin (HA; H5) and neuraminidase (NA; N1) proteins from the genotype B3.13 virus, but the internal protein-encoding genes were derived from the PR8 strain, which supports high yields of the vaccine virus in embryonated eggs. As immunodominant T cell epitopes are associated with internal influenza proteins, this mismatch with the genotype B3.13 strain might have limited T cell immunity and could be one reason why vaccination did not achieve complete protective immunity (36). Vaccine delivery route, together with dose and adjuvant optimization, requires further evaluation to determine which factors limited protective immunity in the udder. The dairy goat model established herein provides a platform for HPAI H5Nx vaccine development, screening, and assessing protective efficacy. In addition to improving vaccine design, consideration of cross-protection is necessary given the circulation of the two different H5N1 genotypes in cows. Natural immunity provides limited cross-protection in dairy cows, thus multivalent vaccine approaches are likely needed (21, 22). We propose that the dairy goat model can also be used to evaluate multivalent vaccine approaches given their susceptibility to both genotypes. The smaller stature of dairy goats, relative to dairy cows, allows for greater occupancy within high biocontainment agricultural rooms enabling researchers to use larger group sizes needed for robust group-level comparisons.Inactivated, DNA and mRNA H5N1 vaccines have previously been tested in cows. These vaccines prevented shedding of infectious virus in milk, although, in the absence of viral RNA detection, it is unclear whether sterilizing immunity was achieved (30, 31). Our data emphasize the importance of measuring both infectious virus and viral RNA to provide a complete picture of replication dynamics.In this study, infection-induced immunity in ADJ goats conferred protection against reinfection, consistent with our observations in dairy cows (20). Reexposing ADJ goats to H5N1 by inoculating into the left mammary gland did not result in clinical mastitis, milk production losses, or viral shedding; neither viral RNA nor infectious virus was detected. Before reexposing ADJ goats to H5N1, VN antibodies were not readily detected in left gland milk, yet all goats were protected from reinfection. However, anti-H5 IgG antibodies were detected in left gland milk of all ADJ goats, confirming the presence of antigen-specific antibodies in milk before rechallenge. This suggests that even low levels of antibodies correlate with protective immunity, similar to our observations in dairy cows, where low milk VN titers of 1:10 were associated with protection (20). Cell-mediated immunity in the udder likely plays an important role in immune protection, but to what extent remains to be determined. Defining the contribution of T cell–mediated responses to H5N1 infection is warranted to provide a complete understanding of host immunity.The emergence of HPAI H5N1 virus in dairy cows reveals a new mammalian host and tissue tropism that can trigger an avian influenza panzootic and introduces a novel pathway for zoonotic transmission to humans. This ongoing pandemic threat underscores the need for preparedness strategies that block cross-species transmission. Relevant H5N1 mammary infection models, such as the goat model, will become critically important for addressing key knowledge gaps and supporting the development of effective countermeasures to combat this public health threat.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4b has spread globally since 2020, resulting in extensive mortality in wild birds and commercial poultry (1–3). During its circulation, this clade has undergone extensive reassortment and expanded into an unusually broad host range, including many mammalian species (2, 4, 5). In 2024, HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13 was detected in dairy cows in the USA, introduced through a single transmission event from wild birds, followed by widespread cow-to-cow transmission within dairy herds in the USA (6). Historically, cattle were not affected by influenza A virus as evidenced by the rare occurrence of natural infections (7, 8). Since the initial HPAI H5N1 detection, three separate introductions to dairy cattle in the USA have been detected, all of clade 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1, the dominant genotype in North American flyways (9, 10). Genotype B3.13 emerged in North America through reassortment between Eurasian 2.3.4.4.b lineage A1 viruses and circulating low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI), incorporating four segments from lineage A1 (PA, HA, NA, and M) and four segments from LPAI. Similarly, genotype D1.1 comprises four 2.3.4.4b A3 lineage segments (HA, PB1, M, and NS) and four from North American LPAI (11). To date, H5N1 has been confirmed in 1088 dairy cattle herds in 19 US states (12). Nearly all of these detections have been associated with genotype B3.13, whereas the genotype D1.1 spillovers have been reported in a small number of herds and were quickly contained (10). Experimental studies show that the virus primarily replicates in the bovine mammary gland, leading to acute mastitis and shedding of infectious virus in milk (13, 14). HPAI H5N1 outbreaks in dairy herds have major economic impacts for producers due to decreased milk yield that can persist for up to 2 months postinfection, increased culling due to reproductive issues and losses in productivity, and herd-replacement costs (14). HPAI H5N1 was likely introduced to other US dairy herds due to transport of infected cattle (6). Cow-to-cow transmission is thought to occur through the use of contaminated milking equipment, although this has not been recapitulated under experimental settings and additional transmission routes could be involved (6, 15). HPAI H5N1–infected dairy cows have been responsible for further transmission to nearby commercial poultry flocks, barn cats, humans working in close proximity to infected cows, and wildlife such as raccoons and birds, demonstrating that dairy cows can both sustain a panzootic and act as a new transmission pathway for HPAI H5N1 to humans (6, 13). In humans, previous HPAI H5N1 infections acquired from wild birds have been associated with high mortality rates; however, the 41 reported human cases linked to cattle exposure all resulted in mild respiratory-like illness and conjunctivitis (16–18). This increased circulation of HPAI in mammals always raises concerns of mammalian adaptations or reassortment with seasonal influenza viruses that can increase fitness and enable transmission in humans, potentially leading to a serious public health threat (19).We previously showed that experimental H5N1 infection of dairy cows induced natural immunity, which included virus-specific antibodies in milk that neutralized high titers of H5N1 and conferred protection against reinfection (20). Natural immunity in dairy cows persists for at least 1 year, as evidenced by protection against homologous experimental challenge, and is associated with neutralizing antibodies in milk (21, 22). These observations conceptually support that vaccines can be developed that elicit durable and protective immune responses in the udder (23).Conducting HPAI research in cows requires high biocontainment agricultural facilities, and the physical space requirements for these large ruminants exclude many laboratories from performing HPAI studies in the natural host. Goats are a small ruminant that are susceptible to HPAI and have mammary gland architecture comparable to dairy cows, therefore representing a potential surrogate model (24–27). In both species, immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibodies are transferred transepithelially from the blood to the milk and peripherally derived lymphocytes traffic to the mammary gland (28, 29). This supports that parenteral vaccination can generate immune responses that protect the mammary gland. In two separate studies, parenteral vaccination of dairy cows with either an mRNA, DNA, or inactivated virus vaccine induced serum and milk neutralizing antibodies, and no infectious virus was detected in milk following homologous intramammary challenge (30, 31). However, these studies did not report whether vaccination protected cows from milk production losses after challenge or measure viral RNA to confirm the absence of virus in milk. Further refinement of H5N1 vaccine strategies will benefit from a small ruminant surrogate model to support larger sample sizes and provides advantages in animal handling, costs, and safety when working with this high consequence pathogen.Here, we establish dairy goats as a relevant model for HPAI H5N1 mammary infection, bridging a major research gap between large ruminant animals and conventional laboratory models (i.e., mice and ferrets), which differ substantially in their mammary gland architecture. This model provides a biologically relevant species to interrogate existing and emerging H5Nx virus pathogenesis, host immune responses, and countermeasures. title_original: A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a caprine mammary infection model to investigate the pathogenesis and immune response to highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, addressing the need for a relevant animal model to study viral transmission and disease progression in livestock.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved seven goats acclimated for 7 days, with three vaccinated subcutaneously in the neck and three receiving adjuvant alone. One milking machine was dedicated to each vaccinated and unvaccinated cohort, and all procedures were conducted in CL3 laboratories.
analysis.methods: Goats were inoculated with HPAI H5N1 genotypes D1.1 and B3.13, and viral load was measured using TCID50 assays. Serum and milk samples were collected for virus neutralization and ELISA tests, with clinical scoring based on rectal temperatures and signs of respiration, depression, and mastitis.
analysis.main_results: Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. The vaccine group showed reduced clinical signs and viral shedding compared to the adjuvant-only group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of the model's utility in studying H5N1 pathogenesis and immune response, highlighting its potential for vaccine development and efficacy testing.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of vaccines and the understanding of H5N1 transmission in livestock, which is critical for preventing zoonotic spread and ensuring food safety.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its small sample size and the use of a single animal species, but the results are supported by direct observations and validated protocols, providing moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a caprine mammary infection model to investigate the pathogenesis and immune response to highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1. Seven goats were acclimated and divided into vaccinated and adjuvant-only groups. Inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotypes D1.1 and B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding. The vaccinated group showed reduced clinical signs and viral shedding. The model's utility for vaccine development and efficacy testing was highlighted, though its small sample size and limited host scope may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to direct observations and validated methods.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及七只山羊,经过 7 天的适应,其中三只山羊在颈部皮下注射疫苗,三只只接受佐剂。每只接种疫苗和未接种疫苗的 队列研究 都有一台挤奶机,所有程序均在 CL3 实验室进行。
elements_zh.methods: 山羊接种 HPAI H5N1 基因型 D1.1 和 B3.13,并使用 TCID50 测定法测量病毒载量。收集血清和乳汁样本进行病毒中和和 ELISA 测试,并根据直肠温度和呼吸、抑郁和乳腺炎体征进行临床评分。
elements_zh.main_results: 乳房内接种 HPAI H5N1 基因型 D1.1 和 B3.13 会导致急性乳腺炎、产奶量下降和牛奶中病毒大量脱落。与仅使用佐剂的组相比,疫苗 组的临床症状和病毒脱落有所减少。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为该模型在研究 H5N1 发病机制 和 免疫应答 中的实用性的证据,强调了其在 疫苗 开发和功效测试中的潜力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 疫苗 的开发和对牲畜中 H5N1 传播 的理解提供了信息,这对于防止人畜共患传播和确保食品安全至关重要。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和使用单一动物物种的限制,但结果得到了直接观察和经过验证的方案的支持,为研究结果提供了适度的可信度。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a caprine mammary infection model to investigate the pathogenesis and immune response to highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, addressing the need for a relevant animal model to study viral transmission and disease progression in livestock.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved seven goats acclimated for 7 days, with three vaccinated subcutaneously in the neck and three receiving adjuvant alone. One milking machine was dedicated to each vaccinated and unvaccinated cohort, and all procedures were conducted in CL3 laboratories.
analysis_en.methods: Goats were inoculated with HPAI H5N1 genotypes D1.1 and B3.13, and viral load was measured using TCID50 assays. Serum and milk samples were collected for virus neutralization and ELISA tests, with clinical scoring based on rectal temperatures and signs of respiration, depression, and mastitis.
analysis_en.main_results: Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. The vaccine group showed reduced clinical signs and viral shedding compared to the adjuvant-only group.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of the model's utility in studying H5N1 pathogenesis and immune response, highlighting its potential for vaccine development and efficacy testing.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of vaccines and the understanding of H5N1 transmission in livestock, which is critical for preventing zoonotic spread and ensuring food safety.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its small sample size and the use of a single animal species, but the results are supported by direct observations and validated protocols, providing moderate confidence in the findings.

full_text: IntroductionScutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb widely used for its heat-clearing and detoxifying properties, has shown broad-spectrum antiviral potential. However, its anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.MethodsIn this study, the anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms of S. barbata extract were investigated using H1N1-infected MDCK cells and BALB/c mice. Transcriptomic analysis followed by mRNA and protein-level validation was performed to characterize its molecular effects, while UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS was used to identify blood-absorbed constituents. Potential active compounds were subsequently screened by integrating the absorbed constituents with network pharmacology and further validated in vitro and in vivo.ResultsS. barbata extract markedly inhibited H1N1 replication in MDCK cells (IC50 = 42.87 μg/mL; CC50 > 500 μg/mL) and reduced viral burden and pulmonary inflammation in infected mice. Mechanistically, S. barbata treatment suppressed the Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, and chemokine signaling pathways, suggesting coordinated regulation of antiviral and inflammatory responses. Among the blood-absorbed constituents, baicalein and chrysoeriol were identified as key candidate active compounds and exhibited potent anti-H1N1 activity in vitro and in vivo (IC50 = 13.80 and 11.10 μM, respectively).DiscussionCollectively, these findings demonstrate that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 effects through a combination of direct inhibition of viral replication and modulation of excessive inflammatory responses, with baicalein and chrysoeriol representing important contributors to its antiviral activity. Materials and methodsMaterialsChrysoeriol (C861251) was obtained from Macklin (Shanghai, China), and baicalein (B20571) was purchased from Yuan Ye Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, 812207), fetal bovine serum (FBS, 10270-106), 0.25% trypsin–EDTA (2323363), phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, BYHC1713), and Opti-MEM medium (31985070) were all supplied by Gibco (Massachusetts, USA). MDCK cells (as a host of H1N1) and IA V [A/Puerto Rico/8/1934(H1N1)] were provided by the Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences (Jinan, China). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits for TNF-α (JL10484), IL-1β (JL18442), IL-6 (JL20268), IL-2 (JL20256), IFN-γ (JL10967), and IL-4 (JL20266) were obtained from Shanghai Jianglai Biotechnology Co., Ltd., (Shanghai, China). The anti-influenza A virus nucleoprotein antibody (ab20343) was purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies, including FITC anti-mouse CD4 (116004), PE anti-mouse IL-4 (504104), APC anti-mouse IFN-γ (505809), and APC anti-mouse CD8b (Ly-3) (126614), were supplied by BioLegend (California, USA).Sample preparationThe extract of S. barbata was prepared using a water extraction method. Briefly, 100 g of dried herb powder was mixed with 1,000 mL of deionized water and subjected to ultrasonic-assisted extraction at 250 W for 1 h. The resulting extract was filtered, concentrated under reduced pressure, and lyophilized to yield a dry powder. For subsequent experiments, the lyophilized extract was reconstituted according to its experimental application: dissolved in Opti-MEM medium for in vitro cellular assays and in PBS buffer for in vivo animal studies. Both solutions were further diluted to the required working concentrations for pharmacodynamic evaluation.Study on anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vitroMDCK cells were treated with varying concentrations of S. barbata extract and oseltamivir phosphate (OP) for 48 h. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay to determine the 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50) for both agents. The highest tested concentration that maintained cell viability above 90% was defined as the non-cytotoxic concentration for subsequent experiments. For viral infection studies, MDCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells/mL (100 μL per well) and cultured for 24 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Following incubation, the culture medium was removed, and cell monolayers were washed twice with PBS. Cells were then infected with H1N1 virus (100 TCID50/well) in Opti-MEM medium supplemented with 1,000 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 μg/mL TPCK-trypsin, while simultaneously being treated with different concentrations of either S. barbata extract or OP. After 48 h of incubation, cell viability was measured using the MTT assay. full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionScutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb widely used for its heat-clearing and detoxifying properties, has shown broad-spectrum antiviral potential. However, its anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.MethodsIn this study, the anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms of S. barbata extract were investigated using H1N1-infected MDCK cells and BALB/c mice. Transcriptomic analysis followed by mRNA and protein-level validation was performed to characterize its molecular effects, while UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS was used to identify blood-absorbed constituents. Potential active compounds were subsequently screened by integrating the absorbed constituents with network pharmacology and further validated in vitro and in vivo.ResultsS. barbata extract markedly inhibited H1N1 replication in MDCK cells (IC50 = 42.87 μg/mL; CC50 > 500 μg/mL) and reduced viral burden and pulmonary inflammation in infected mice. Mechanistically, S. barbata treatment suppressed the Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, and chemokine signaling pathways, suggesting coordinated regulation of antiviral and inflammatory responses. Among the blood-absorbed constituents, baicalein and chrysoeriol were identified as key candidate active compounds and exhibited potent anti-H1N1 activity in vitro and in vivo (IC50 = 13.80 and 11.10 μM, respectively).DiscussionCollectively, these findings demonstrate that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 effects through a combination of direct inhibition of viral replication and modulation of excessive inflammatory responses, with baicalein and chrysoeriol representing important contributors to its antiviral activity.

full_text_sections.results: ResultsIn vitro antiviral activity of S. barbataIn vitro assays demonstrated that S. barbata and OP exhibited dose-dependent inhibitory effects against H1N1 infection in MDCK cells (Figures 1A, B). The calculated IC50 values of S. barbata and OP were 42.87 and 7.02 μg⋅mL–1, respectively. Both the viral load (Figure 1C) and NP fluorescence intensity (green signal) were significantly lower in the S. barbata treatment group compared with the model group (Figure 1D), indicating that S. barbata markedly inhibited viral replication within H1N1-infected MDCK cells.FIGURE 1In vitro anti-IAV H1N1 assays. Antiviral activity of S. barbata (A) and OP (B) against H1N1 in vitro; viral load in cell supernatant (C) and NP protein expression in MDCK cells (D) (n = 3). ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001 indicate significant differences compared with the model group.Panel A shows a line graph of S. barbata concentration versus percent cell viability and viral inhibition rate, indicating an IC50 of 42.87 micrograms per milliliter. Panel B presents a similar line graph for OP with an IC50 of 7.02 micrograms per milliliter. Panel C is a scatter plot comparing relative expression of H1N1 NP mRNA across five treatment groups, with significant differences marked by asterisks. Panel D contains fifteen fluorescence microscopy images arranged in three rows and five columns showing cell samples under different treatments, labeled as control, H1N1, OP, S. barbata 200, and S. barbata 100 micrograms per milliliter.In vivo antiviral efficacy of S. barbataFollowing intranasal infection with 0.8 LD50 of H1N1 virus, mice in the model group exhibited progressive body weight loss and clinical symptoms such as ruffled fur and reduced activity starting on day 4 post-infection. These effects were notably alleviated in the S. barbata and OP treatment groups (Figure 2A). On day 6 post-infection, mice were euthanized, and the lung, spleen, and thymus were collected and weighed to calculate organ indices. Compared with the control group, the lung index of infected mice significantly increased (Figure 2B), while the thymus (Figure 2C), and spleen indices (Figure 2D) decreased. S. barbata treatment significantly reduced the lung index while elevating spleen and thymus indices relative to the model group. qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the mRNA expression levels of four H1N1 genes–Hemagglutinin (HA) (Figure 2E), neuraminidase (NA) (Figure 2F), M2 (Figure 2G) and NP (Figure 2H)–were markedly decreased in lung tissues from S. barbata-treated mice compared with the model group, suggesting suppression of viral replication in vivo. NP protein expression in lung tissues (I). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, and ****P < 0.0001 indicate significant differences compared with the model group; ns indicates no significant difference.Scientific figure with eight graphs (A-H) and a panel of fluorescence microscopy images (I) comparing groups labeled Control, Model, OP, S. barbata 390 mg/kg, and S. barbata 78 mg/kg. Graphs show host weight change, lung, thymus, spleen indices, and relative mRNA expression of viral genes, with significance indicated by asterisks. Fluorescence images display varying green signal intensities among groups.Effects of S. barbata on lung inflammation and cytokine expressionBased on the analysis of organ indices, S. barbata significantly reduced the lung index in H1N1-infected mice. As the lung index reflects the extent of pulmonary inflammatory infiltration, this finding suggests that S. barbata may alleviate H1N1-induced inflammatory injury in lung tissues. Therefore, we further investigated the inhibitory effect of S. barbata on H1N1-induced inflammatory responses. In the model group, lung tissues showed thickened alveolar septa, narrowed alveolar spaces, focal necrosis of alveolar epithelial cells, extensive inflammatory cell infiltration, and marked vascular congestion. Treatment with S. barbata alleviated alveolar septal thickening and inflammatory infiltration (Figure 3A). In the OP group, alveolar injury and inflammatory infiltration were also improved, though mild vascular congestion was still observed.FIGURE 3The effects of S. barbata on levels of inflammatory in lung tissues and lung lesions were investigated. Histopathological examination (A) (n = 3). The levels of IL-1β (B), IL-4 (C), IL-2 (D), TNF-α (E), IL-6 (F), IFN-γ (G) in lung tissues (n = 6). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, and ****P < 0.0001 indicate significant differences compared with the model group; ns indicates no significant difference.Panel A contains histological images of lung tissue from four experimental groups, displaying differences in tissue structure among control, model, OP, and Scutellaria barbata treated groups. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionDirect and indirect anti-H1N1 effects of S. barbataThe antiviral activity of S. barbata extract against H1N1 infection was first evaluated in an MDCK cell model. The extract exhibited a IC50 of 42.87 μg/mL against H1N1, while showing negligible cytotoxicity toward MDCK cells (CC50 > 500 μg/mL). Within the non-cytotoxic concentration range (100 and 200 μg/mL), S. barbata treatment markedly reduced viral titers in the supernatant and decreased the intracellular expression level of the viral NP. Consistent with the in vitro findings, S. barbata also demonstrated significant protective efficacy against H1N1 infection in vivo. Direct antiviral effects are generally defined as interference with viral proliferation processes, including adsorption, penetration, replication, assembly, or release, or by damaging viral structural proteins. HA and NA are characteristic surface glycoproteins of H1N1, while NP and matrix protein M2 serve as core structural proteins. RT-qPCR analysis revealed that S. barbata significantly downregulated the mRNA expression of HA, NA, NP, and M2 in mouse lung tissues, showing a consistent inhibitory trend across all four genes. These results suggest that S. barbata exerts a direct inhibitory effect on H1N1 viral replication.In addition to direct antiviral action, S. barbata also exerts indirect effects by alleviating virus-induced tissue injury and modulating host immune responses. Following H1N1 invasion, infected mice typically exhibit pulmonary congestion, edema, and increased lung mass. The lung index serves as a key indicator of pulmonary inflammation and is widely used to evaluate the anti-H1N1 efficacy of candidate drugs. Moreover, the developmental state of immune organs such as the spleen and thymus reflects the overall immune competence of the host. H1N1 infection generally reduces the spleen and thymus indices due to excessive immune cell consumption. S. barbata administration significantly decreased the lung index while restoring the spleen and thymus indices, indicating that the extract protects the host through immunoregulatory mechanisms.Upon influenza virus infection, the host immune system releases a variety of cytokines to inhibit viral replication and regulate immunity. However, excessive cytokine secretion can trigger uncontrolled inflammation and tissue injury, a phenomenon often referred to as a “cytokine storm.” Thus, suppressing hyperinflammatory cytokine release is critical for mitigating H1N1-induced lung damage. Overexpression of IL-1β promotes excessive recruitment and activation of neutrophils and macrophages, while IL-6 facilitates neutrophil chemotaxis and local infiltration. TNF-α induces leukocyte migration and promotes degranulation of granulocytes, amplifying the inflammatory cascade. Elevated levels of IL-1β, IFN-γ, IL-6, and TNF-α have been correlated with the severity of H1N1 infection in clinical cases. In our study, S. barbata significantly reduced the levels of these pro-inflammatory cytokines in lung homogenates, consistent with histopathological findings showing alleviated pulmonary injury. IL-2 is a key cytokine that promotes the differentiation of CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic T lymphocytes during viral infection (Zhou et al., 2021). Our results showed that S. barbata treatment significantly decreased IL-2 levels in the lungs of H1N1-infected mice. Therefore, we further explored its regulatory effects on CD4+ and CD8+ T cell populations. CD8+ T cells play a direct role in killing infected cells, whereas CD4+ T cells enhance the effector functions of innate immune cells and B cells. An imbalance in the CD4+/CD8+ ratio has been associated with increased severity of H1N1-induced pneumonia. Flow cytometry revealed that S. barbata decreased the proportion of CD4+ T cells in the spleen without significantly affecting CD8+ T cells, suggesting that the extract may suppress overactivation of CD4+ T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, S. barbata partially restored the Th1/Th2 balance by increasing both Th1 and Th2 subpopulations, indicating a bidirectional regulatory effect. Interestingly, despite the overall increase in CD4+ T cell proportion in the model group, both Th1 and Th2 subsets were reduced, implying expansion of other CD4+ subpopulations–a phenomenon warranting further investigation.Molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-H1N1 effects of S. barbataTranscriptomic analysis provided deeper insight into the molecular basis of S. barbata’s anti-H1N1 activity. GO enrichment analysis indicated that the DEGs after S. barbata treatment were mainly involved in biological processes such as regulation of inflammatory responses, positive regulation of innate immunity, and leukocyte migration. The enriched cellular components included “ficolin-1-rich granule” and “ficolin-1-rich granule lumen.” Ficolin-1-rich granules store and release Ficolin-1 upon stimulation; Ficolin-1 functions as a soluble pattern recognition receptor that recognizes pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and activates the complement system via the lectin pathway, thereby participating in innate immune signaling.Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment further revealed that the toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathway was the most significantly modulated pathway following S. barbata treatment. During IAV infection, viral RNA within airway and alveolar epithelial cells activates TLRs, leading to the induction of interferon regulatory factors and type I interferons (IFN-α/β). This activation can subsequently trigger the NF-κB pathway, promoting the expression of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines. While these responses are essential for viral clearance, excessive activation results in tissue injury. Our data indicate that S. barbata alleviates H1N1-induced pathology by suppressing the overactivation of the TLR and NF-κB pathways. These findings were further validated by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemical analyses, which confirmed the downregulation of key genes in the TLR and chemokine signaling pathways.Identification and validation of the active compounds responsible for the anti-H1N1 activityFollowing oral administration, most herbal components undergo absorption, distribution, and metabolism before reaching their target tissues. Pharmacological activity is generally mediated by prototype or metabolized compounds that enter systemic circulation. Using UPLC-MS, we identified 122 blood-absorbed constituents of S. barbata. By integrating network pharmacology and transcriptomic analyses, we intersected the predicted targets of these compounds with DEGs identified in the transcriptomic data, constructing a “S. barbata–compound–target–pathway–H1N1” interaction network. Among these, baicalein and chrysoeriol exhibited the highest degree values in the network, indicating their central regulatory roles. These two flavonoids were associated with multiple antiviral and immune-related pathways, including the influenza A pathway, chemokine signaling pathway, toll-like receptor signaling pathway, and downstream NF-κB pathway. Subsequent in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that both baicalein and chrysoeriol possessed potent inhibitory effects against H1N1 infection, validating the network-based predictions.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInfluenza A virus (IAV), a member of the genus Influenza virus within the family Orthomyxoviridae, is an enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus (Zeng et al., 2016). Since the 20th century, IAV has caused multiple global pandemics, at least three of which were closely associated with the H1N1 subtype (Krammer et al., 2018). The most recent pandemic, the 2009 H1N1 “swine flu” outbreak, resulted in at least 16,000 deaths worldwide. In addition to pandemics, IAV exhibits a pronounced seasonal epidemic pattern. Although seasonal strains generally display lower pathogenicity than emerging pandemic variants, they can still lead to severe lower respiratory tract infections and extensive lung injury. According to estimates by Iuliano et al. (2018) seasonal influenza causes approximately 291,243–645,832 deaths globally each year; among 92 surveyed countries, 9,243–105,690 annual deaths in children under 5 years of age were attributed to IAV infection (Iuliano et al., 2018). Furthermore, Wang et al. (2020) reported that in 2018, around 10 million children under 5 years old worldwide developed influenza-associated acute lower respiratory tract infections, resulting in approximately 870,000 hospitalizations and 35,000 deaths.Following IAV infection, the host’s innate immune system is rapidly activated. Infected host cells recognize viral pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through various pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), thereby initiating innate immune signaling pathways. Once viral RNA enters the cytoplasm, it activates three principal intracellular immune pathways: the retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) pathway, the toll-like receptor (TLR) pathway, and the inflammasome pathway, all of which contribute to antiviral innate immunity. During the early phase of IAV infection, immune responses occur primarily in infected airway and alveolar epithelial cells. Viral RNA activates the TLR signaling pathway, inducing the expression of key signaling molecules that promote the activation of interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) and enhance the transcription of type I interferons (IFN-α/β). Moreover, activation of this pathway can further stimulate the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling cascade, leading to the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. The combined effects of type I interferons, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and the activation and differentiation of cytotoxic T cells ultimately contribute to viral clearance (Jagger et al., 2012).Although traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) does not include the concept of “virus,” antiviral therapy within TCM dates back to the Han dynasty, notably to Zhang Zhongjing’s Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases. According to TCM theory, IAV infection belongs to the category of “Warm Diseases” and is closely related to pulmonary disorders caused by “external heat pathogens” (Cao et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2009). TCM herbal medicines are characterized by multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway mechanisms. Their active extracts can inhibit viral replication, disrupt viral structure, regulate immune balance, and maintain systemic homeostasis, reflecting the holistic regulatory principles of TCM (Zhang et al., 2013).In our previous screening of herbal medicines with anti-H1N1 activity, the aqueous extract of Scutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata) exhibited significant antiviral potential. S. barbata, a member of the Lamiaceae family and the genus S. barbata is the dried whole herb traditionally used for its heat-clearing, detoxifying, blood-stasis-resolving, hemostatic, diuretic, and anti-edematous properties. Modern pharmacological studies have demonstrated that heat-clearing and detoxifying herbs generally possess strong antiviral potential. Extracts of S. barbata have been shown to alleviate SARS-CoV-2–induced acute lung injury by inhibiting viral replication and modulating immune responses (Ran et al., 2025); its combined extract with Hedyotis diffusa suppresses hepatitis B virus–related hepatocellular carcinoma growth by regulating circular RNA (circRNA) expression (Yang et al., 2021); diterpenoids isolated from S. barbata display inhibitory activity against Epstein–Barr virus lytic replication (Wu et al., 2015); and its total flavonoid fraction exhibits anti-parainfluenza virus activity (Shan-Shan et al., 2009).Based on these findings, the present study established H1N1-infected MDCK cell and BALB/c mouse models to systematically evaluate the inhibitory effects of S. barbata extract against IAV (H1N1 subtype). The results demonstrated that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 activity by directly suppressing viral replication and modulating anti-inflammatory and immune-related signaling pathways. Baicalein and chrysoeriol were confirmed to be key constituents responsible for the antiviral activity of S. barbata. Sample preparationThe extract of S. barbata was prepared using a water extraction method. Briefly, 100 g of dried herb powder was mixed with 1,000 mL of deionized water and subjected to ultrasonic-assisted extraction at 250 W for 1 h. The resulting extract was filtered, concentrated under reduced pressure, and lyophilized to yield a dry powder. For subsequent experiments, the lyophilized extract was reconstituted according to its experimental application: dissolved in Opti-MEM medium for in vitro cellular assays and in PBS buffer for in vivo animal studies. Both solutions were further diluted to the required working concentrations for pharmacodynamic evaluation. Study on anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vitroMDCK cells were treated with varying concentrations of S. barbata extract and oseltamivir phosphate (OP) for 48 h. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay to determine the 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50) for both agents. The highest tested concentration that maintained cell viability above 90% was defined as the non-cytotoxic concentration for subsequent experiments. For viral infection studies, MDCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells/mL (100 μL per well) and cultured for 24 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Following incubation, the culture medium was removed, and cell monolayers were washed twice with PBS. Cells were then infected with H1N1 virus (100 TCID50/well) in Opti-MEM medium supplemented with 1,000 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 μg/mL TPCK-trypsin, while simultaneously being treated with different concentrations of either S. barbata extract or OP. After 48 h of incubation, cell viability was measured using the MTT assay. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values for S. barbata and OP against H1N1 viral infection were calculated according to the Reed-Muench method (Chen et al., 2010; Geng et al., 2019).MDCK cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 8 × 104 cells per well and cultured until full confluence was reached. The cell monolayers were then washed twice with PBS and replenished with fresh Opti-MEM medium. Subsequently, the cells were treated with either S. barbata extract or OP, followed by immediate infection with H1N1 virus at a dose of 100 TCID50 per well. The infected cells were maintained at 37 °C under 5% CO2 for 24 h. To quantify viral gene expression, cells subjected to the above treatment were harvested after three freeze-thaw cycles, and the supernatant was collected following centrifugation. The mRNA expression level of the H1N1 NP gene in the supernatant was detected by Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). For the analysis of viral protein expression, MDCK cells grown on coverslips in 12-well plates were treated and infected under identical conditions as described above. After 24 h of infection, the coverslips were collected, and the expression level of H1N1 NP protein in MDCK cells was determined by immunofluorescence assay. title_original: Exploration of the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus, addressing the need for understanding its antiviral properties and potential therapeutic applications.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved in vitro assays using MDCK cells and in vivo experiments on mice, with the latter divided into control, model, and treatment groups. The treatment group received Scutellaria barbata extract, while the model group was exposed to the virus.
analysis.methods: The study used enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits to measure cytokine levels, MTT assay to assess cytotoxicity, and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) to detect viral gene expression. Immunofluorescence assays and histopathological examination were also employed to analyze viral protein expression and tissue changes.
analysis.main_results: In vitro assays demonstrated that Scutellaria barbata suppressed viral gene expression and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels. The treatment also showed effects on the expression of antiviral and inflammatory pathways in infected cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that Scutellaria barbata may modulate antiviral and inflammatory responses through suppression of key signaling pathways, offering a novel perspective on its potential therapeutic use against influenza A (H1N1) virus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the mechanisms of Scutellaria barbata's antiviral activity, which could inform future research on natural compounds for influenza treatment and support the development of targeted therapies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on in vitro and in vivo models, which may not fully represent human influenza dynamics. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on experimental findings without direct clinical outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus. It employs in vitro and in vivo models to assess the antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects of the extract. The results indicate that Scutellaria barbata suppresses viral gene expression and modulates inflammatory pathways. These findings suggest potential therapeutic applications but are based on experimental models, limiting their direct clinical relevance. The study contributes to understanding natural antiviral agents but lacks human data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在探索半枝莲对抗甲型H1N1流感病毒的机制和活性化合物,满足了解其抗病毒药物特性和潜在治疗应用的需要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及使用 MDCK 细胞进行的体外测定和小鼠体内实验,后者分为对照组、模型组和 治疗 组。治疗组接受半枝莲提取物,而模型组则暴露于病毒。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用酶联免疫吸附测定(ELISA)试剂盒测量细胞因子水平,使用MTT测定评估细胞毒性,并使用定量实时PCR(qRT-PCR)检测病毒基因表达。还采用免疫荧光测定和组织病理学检查来分析病毒蛋白表达和组织变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 体外试验表明半枝莲可抑制病毒基因表达并降低炎症细胞因子水平。治疗 还显示出对感染细胞中 抗病毒药物 表达和炎症途径的影响。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,半枝莲可能通过抑制关键信号通路来调节 抗病毒药物 和炎症反应,为其对抗甲型 H1N1 流感病毒的潜在治疗用途提供了新的视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果提供了对半枝莲 抗病毒药物 活性机制的深入了解,这可以为未来针对流感 治疗 的天然化合物的研究提供信息,并支持靶向治疗的开发。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖体外和体内模型而受到限制,这些模型可能无法完全代表人类流感动态。证据是中等的,因为它基于没有直接临床结果的实验​​结果。

analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果提供了对半枝莲 抗病毒药物 活性机制的深入了解,这可以为未来针对流感 治疗 的天然化合物的研究提供信息,并支持靶向治疗的开发。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖体外和体内模型而受到限制,这些模型可能无法完全代表人类流感动态。证据是中等的,因为它基于没有直接临床结果的实验​​结果。

title: Shifts in acute respiratory pathogen epidemiology: an 8-year surveillance study in Hangzhou, China (2018–2025)

source_records.title: Shifts in acute respiratory pathogen epidemiology: an 8-year surveillance study in Hangzhou, China (2018–2025)

full_text: AbstractObjectivesTo analyze the epidemiological characteristics of six common respiratory pathogens in cases of Acute Respiratory Tract Infection (ARTI) in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025, to provide a basis for clinical diagnosis and treatment, as well as public health prevention and control.MethodsA multicenter retrospective study was conducted. Data from 81,974 ARTI cases from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou City between January 2018 and December 2025 were collected. Cases with positive test results were analyzed for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP), and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.ResultsAmong 81,974 patients, a total of 33,350 cases tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positive rate of 40.68%. MP (19.56%) and FluA (16.93%) were the most prevalent pathogens. The positivity rates of each pathogen showed statistically significant differences across the three stages before, during, and after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (all P < 0.001). Compared with the pre-COVID-19 pandemic period (2018–2019), the positive rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022), and then experienced a sharp “revenge rebound” in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) (for example, the positive rate of MP rebounded from 5.43% to 21.09%). In contrast, the positive rates of RSV, ADV, and CP showed a persistent state of inhibition, but the absolute number of cases far exceeded that of before the COVID-19 pandemic. MP had the highest infection rate among 6– < 12 years old (38.31%), whereas FluA was more common in adults. The epidemiological distribution showed obvious seasonal heterogeneity: FluA/FluB/RSV were more prevalent in winter, MP was active in autumn, and ADV was more prevalent in summer. The co-infection rate was 7.22% (5,922 cases), and the most common combination was FluA + MP, accounting for 53.82% of all co-infections.ConclusionFrom 2018 to 2025, the pathogen spectrum of ARTI in Hangzhou was mainly composed of MP and FluA. The COVID-19 pandemic and related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) have had a profound and heterogeneous impact on the epidemic pattern of respiratory pathogens. FluA, FluB, and MP showed the characteristics of “suppression-retaliatory rebound.” In the post-COVID-19 pandemic era, the activity of pathogens has clear seasonal, age, and gender distribution patterns, and the rate of mixed infections is high. The research results suggest that a dynamic monitoring system needs to be established, and targeted prevention and control measures should be implemented for key individuals and pathogens during high-incidence seasons.Keywords: Acute Respiratory Tract Infection, epidemiological characteristics, Hangzhou, influenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, pathogen spectrum 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study populationThis study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens—influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), RSV, adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP)—among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, and to evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics. A total of 81,974 patients from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou seven medical institutions in Hangzhou (see Supplementary Table 1 for details) between January 2018 and December 2025 were selected as study subjects. The diagnostic criteria for cases were as follows: pediatric cases were defined according to the Practical Pediatrics (Zhu Futang, 8th edition) (8), while adult cases were defined according to the Expert consensus on the diagnosis, treatment, and infection control of acute respiratory infections in adult outpatient and emergency departments (9), including: (1) Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI): presence of ≥2 symptoms—fever (body temperature ≥38 °C), cough, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, or sneezing—with a duration of ≤ 7 days. (2) Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI): Clinical signs: increased respiratory rate, moist rales/whistling sounds in the lungs, or tracheal retractions; Radiological evidence (X-ray/CT): signs of pneumonia/bronchitis (e.g., patchy infiltrates, atelectasis). Exclusion criteria: Incomplete clinical data, incomplete pathogen detection results, or duplicate records. Clinical data from 1,431,696 individuals undergoing respiratory pathogen screening were collected in this study. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we excluded entries with incomplete pathogen detection, removed duplicate data from repeated hospitalizations and repeated outpatient visits (1,331,565 cases), as well as duplicate data between outpatient and inpatient records (18,157 cases). Ultimately, a total of 81,974 subjects were included in the statistical analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Flowchart of the study.Flowchart illustrating a retrospective study design, showing data collection from seven medical institutions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, cohort selection process, analysis dimensions, and six key epidemiological outcomes for respiratory pathogen infections.2.2.Data collectionDemographic and clinical data of enrolled cases were collected through the “Xiaoshan Health Data Platform” platform. The determination of infection status was based on any of the following positive test results: positive serum pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, or positive pathogen antigens or nucleic acids detected in respiratory tract samples. This study encompasses six common respiratory pathogens, including FluA, FluB, RSV, ADV, MP, and CP. For all six pathogens, specimen types included nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and blood; detection methods included serological IgM assays, antigen detection, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), with the exception that antigen detection was not included for CP. Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. Only patients with complete test results for all six target pathogens were included in the final analysis.Grouping of study subjects: in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for age-stage division and population age stratification, the study subjects were divided into six age groups: 0– < 3 years (infant and toddler group), 3– < 6 years (preschool group), 6– < 12 years (school-age group), 12– < 18 years (adolescence group), 18– < 60 years (adult group), and ≥60 years (older adult(s) group). According to year span, the subjects were divided into three periods: 2018–2019, 2020–2022, and 2023–2025. Seasonal grouping included spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February of the following year). The chi-square (χ2) two-sided test was used for intergroup comparisons of qualitative data, and a P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.2.3.Statistical analysisData were exported to Excel, and statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.3.2. Normally distributed continuous data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed data are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR). Positivity rates for each study period were calculated as the total number of positive cases divided by the total number of tested cases across all years within that period. Count data are presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square test. All tests were two-sided, and the significance level was set at α = 0.05. Calculation formula: Positive rate (%) = (Number of positive cases detected among the screened population / Total number of screened cases) × 100%. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1907370/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 3.Results3.1.Basic characteristics of the research subjectsAmong 81,974 patients with ARTI, 33,350 were positive for pathogens, with a positivity rate of 40.68%. Specifically, the positive rate for outpatient cases was 44.64% (30,405/68,109), and that for inpatient cases was 19.83% (2,749/13,865). Among the 81,974 ARTI patients screened from 2018 to 2025, the number of cases each year was 1,915, 3,116, 1,086, 1,676, 2,963, 19,630, 31,639, and 19,949, respectively. The pathogen positive rates were 21.78% (417/1,915), 26.03% (811/3,116), 14.09% (153/1,086), 10.80% (181/1,676), 14.21% (421/2,963), 51.08% (10,027/19,630), 39.03% (12,350/31,639), and 44.08% (8,794/19,949), respectively, as shown in Figure 2. There were 41,996 males and 39,978 females, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.05:1. The median age was 24.00 (5.00, 37.00) years.Figure 2The number and positive rate of respiratory pathogens in acute respiratory infection cases in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025.Stacked bar and line chart showing annual positive cases of a disease in outpatients and hospitalized patients from 2018 to 2025, with positive rates peaking in 2023 and 2024 before declining in 2025.Further stratified analysis revealed significant variations in the outpatient-inpatient positivity gap across subgroups (Supplementary Table 2). By age, the largest disparity was observed in children aged 3– < 6 years, with a positivity rate of 59.50% in outpatients compared to 22.44% in inpatients (difference of 36.9 percentage points). By time period, the gap widened markedly in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025: 51.27% vs. 22.93%) compared to the pre-COVID-19 pandemic period (2018–2019: 35.18% vs. 23.57%). By pathogen, Flu A, Flu B, and MP showed higher positivity in outpatients, whereas RSV, ADV, and CP were higher in inpatients.3.2.Analysis of the positive detection status of pathogens and their temporal trendsFrom 2018 to 2025, among the acute respiratory infection cases in Hangzhou, the detection results of six common respiratory pathogens showed that MP had the highest overall positive rate (19.56%, 16,035/81,974), followed by FluA (16.93%, 13,876/81,974). The overall positivity rates of the remaining four pathogens ranged from 0.23% to 7.25%, including FluB (7.25%, 5,946/81,974), RSV (2.45%, 2,007/81,974), ADV (1.85%, 1,518/81,974), and CP (0.23%, 190/81,974).Chi-square tests were performed to assess overall differences in the positive rates of each pathogen across the three period. The results indicated that the differences in the positive rates of each pathogen among the three periods were significant (all P < 0.001). Specifically, the positive rates of FluA, MP, and FluB showed a suppression during the COVID-19 pandemic period and rebounded significantly after the pandemic, presenting a typical “revenge-style epidemic” pattern, whereas, the positive rates of RSV, ADV, and CP showed a persistent state of inhibition, but the absolute number of cases was substantially higher than before the pandemic. The positive rates of MP and FluA from 2020 to 2022 demonstrated a decrease compared to 2018–2019 and from 2023 to 2025, showing an obvious “V-shaped” trend. Among them, the positive rate of MP during the COVID-19 pandemic period (5.43%) decreased by 61.1% compared with that before the pandemic (13.95%), and rebounded to 21.09% after the pandemic, an increase of 288.3% compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period; the positive rate of FluA during the COVID-19 pandemic period (1.57%) decreased by 58.5% compared with that before the pandemic (3.78%), and increased to 19.09% after the pandemic, an increase of 1115.9% compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period. The positive rates of ADV and CP from 2018 to 2019 were higher than those from 2020 to 2022 and from 2023 to 2025. The positive rate of ADV was 5.39% before the pandemic and decreased to 1.55% and 1.63% in the latter two periods, respectively; the positive rate of CP was 1.19% before the pandemic and decreased to 0.05% and 0.18% in the latter two periods, respectively. The positive rates of RSV were 3.08%, 2.90%, and 2.37% in the three periods, respectively, showing a gradual downward trend (P < 0.001). It is worth noting that although the overall positive rate decreased, the number of cases in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) (1,686 cases) was much higher than that before the pandemic (155 cases), suggesting an increase in the absolute number of infected individuals (Table 1 and Figure 3).Table 1Comparison of positive rates of respiratory pathogen antibodies in different time periods.Pathogens2018–2019 year (N = 5,031)2020–2022 year (N = 5,725)2023–2025 year (N = 71,218)χ2 valueP-valueFlu A190 (3.78)90 (1.57)13,596 (19.09)1815.708< 0.001Flu B79 (1.57)135 (2.36)5,732 (8.05)512.402< 0.001RSV155 (3.08)166 (2.90)1,686 (2.37)15.263< 0.001ADV271 (5.39)89 (1.55)1,158 (1.63)368.627< 0.001MP702 (13.95)311 (5.43)15,022 (21.09)933.074< 0.001CP60 (1.19)3 (0.05)127 (0.18)217.617< 0.001Data are presented as N (%). Positivity rates for each study period were calculated as the total number of positive cases divided by the total number of tested cases across all years within that period. χ2 values were derived from 3 (time periods) × 2 (positive/negative) contingency tables for each pathogen independently. Total positive rate was defined as the proportion of cases testing positive for at least one of the six target pathogens. FluA, influenza A virus; FluB, influenza B virus; RSV, respiratory syncytial virus; ADV, adenovirus; MP, Mycoplasma pneumoniae; CP, Chlamydia pneumoniae.Figure 3Monthly positive rate trends of six respiratory pathogens in Hangzhou, 2018–2025. FluA, influenza A virus; FluB, influenza B virus; RSV, respiratory syncytial virus; ADV, adenovirus; MP, Mycoplasma pneumoniae; CP, Chlamydia pneumoniae.Line graph showing positive rates by year from 2018 to 2025 for six respiratory viruses: FluA, FluB, RSV, ADV, MP, and CP. Sections are marked as pre-pandemic (2018-2019), pandemic control (2020-2022), and post-pandemic (2023-2025). MP and FluA rates spike sharply after 2023, while all virus rates drop markedly during the pandemic control period.Upon further analysis of seasonal trends, the total positive detection rate of respiratory pathogens exhibited a fluctuating upward trend across seasons (χ2 = 3335.18, P < 0.001), indicating significant overall seasonal variation. However, pathogen-specific seasonal differences were not uniform: most pathogens showed statistically significant seasonal variation (P < 0.05), while CP exhibited no significant seasonal difference. Specifically, FluA, FluB, and RSV shared a winter-peaking pattern, with the highest positive rates in winter (21.90%, 10.87%, and 2.76%, respectively) and the lowest in summer or autumn. ADV peaked in summer (3.28%) and troughed in winter (1.19%), while MP peaked in autumn (21.62%) and troughed in spring (14.49%). Normally distributed continuous data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed data are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR). Positivity rates for each study period were calculated as the total number of positive cases divided by the total number of tested cases across all years within that period. Count data are presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square test. All tests were two-sided, and the significance level was set at α = 0.05. Calculation formula: Positive rate (%) = (Number of positive cases detected among the screened population / Total number of screened cases) × 100%.
