full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study conducts a multi-center retrospective analysis of a total of 81,974 ARTI cases in Hangzhou from 2018 to 2025, describing the temporal variations in the epidemic patterns of six major respiratory pathogens before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Our data confirm the rebound phenomenon of pathogen activity observed globally in the post-COVID-19 pandemic era. However, the recovery patterns varied markedly across pathogens: Flu A and MP rebounded rapidly to pre- COVID-19 pandemic levels, whereas RSV and ADV exhibited delayed or incomplete recovery. These divergent trajectories resulted in a reshaped epidemiological landscape, characterized by altered seasonal peaks and shifts in the age groups predominantly affected. These findings have important implications for understanding the complexity of the “immunity debt” hypothesis, optimizing clinical practice, and reconstructing the local surveillance and early-warning system.Research findings indicate that there are significant differences in the inhibitory effects of NPIs on common respiratory pathogens. The positive rates of Influenza A (FluA), Influenza B (FluB), and MP were significantly suppressed during the period of epidemic prevention and control from 2020 to 2022, and then showed a sharp “revenge rebound” from 2023 to 2025. In particular, the positive rate of FluA in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (19.09%) was more than five times that before the COVID-19 pandemic (3.78%), representing a rebound increase of over 11-fold compared with the COVID-19 pandemic period (1.57%). This phenomenon is consistent with reports from many countries around the world and is widely attributed to the “immunity debt,” that is, NPIs led to a decrease in natural infections among the population and an accumulation of susceptible individuals. Once the interventions were lifted, the pathogens spread rapidly among the population with immunity gaps (7, 10, 11).However, the decline in the positive rates of ADV, CP, and RSV in this study challenges the view that the single “immune debt” hypothesis can universally explain the dynamics of all pathogens, and reveals the “asymmetry” of the impact of NPIs (12). This disparity is the result of the combined effects of pathogen characteristics, population immunodynamics, and persistent changes in behavioral patterns after the pandemic. Taking ADV as an example, it has multiple transmission routes such as droplet, fecal-oral, and contact (13), this niche breadth may have buffered the impact of NPIs, preventing the complete interruption of its transmission during the pandemic and thus avoiding the accumulation of a large susceptible population like that of influenza viruses and MP (14). The latter two are highly dependent on droplet transmission and are strongly suppressed under NPIs, which in turn leads to a “revenge epidemic” after the lifting of the interventions. It is worth noting that the interpretation of the “decline in the positive rate” requires extra caution. Although the positive rates of ADV, CP, and RSV show a persistent state of inhibition, the absolute number of detected cases during the post-COVID-19 pandemic period (2023–2025) far exceeds the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level (15–17). This strongly suggests that the simple positive rate may underestimate the actual intensity of community transmission and disease burden of this pathogen in the post-COVID-19 pandemic stage. The reasons for this phenomenon may include: the recovery and increase in the overall number of medical consultations after the pandemic, the improvement in the willingness to undergo testing, and the sample dilution effect caused by the co-circulation with other pathogens (such as MP, FluA) (18, 19). Therefore, our data indicate that the evolution of respiratory pathogens in the “post-pandemic era” is not simply a “return to the baseline,” but rather a profound “restructuring of ecological niches.” With their high transmission efficiency, MP and influenza viruses have significantly increased their epidemiological weight in the context of expanded susceptible pools and the restoration of transmission conditions; while other pathogens have their activity levels reshaped either due to their transmission characteristics or because of sustained behavioral suppression (20). This suggests that in the surveillance during the “post-COVID-19 pandemic era,” it is necessary to combine multi-dimensional indicators such as the positive rate and the absolute number of cases, and take into account confounding factors such as changes in medical seeking behavior to more accurately assess the real epidemic situation and disease burden of various pathogens.The stratified outpatient-inpatient comparison further illustrates how healthcare-seeking behavior shapes surveillance data. The universal lower inpatient positivity rate across age groups likely reflects that inpatients include more non-infectious admissions and prior antibiotic use. The widening gap post- COVID-19 pandemic suggests a surge in mild community infections seeking outpatient care. Notably, RSV and ADV were higher in inpatients, consistent with their tendency to cause more severe disease requiring hospitalization (21, 22).This study clearly identifies that MP has become the pathogen with the highest positive rate (19.56%) among ARTI cases in the Hangzhou area, far exceeding that of FluA (16.93%). Age distribution analysis showed that MP infection peaked in children aged 6– < 12 years (38.31%), consistent with recent reports from multiple domestic regions (23, 24). The higher overall positivity of MP compared to RSV in our cohort reflects their distinct age-specific ecological niches rather than diminished clinical relevance of RSV. Age-stratified analysis (Table 4) revealed that MP positivity increased markedly with age, peaking in school-aged children (6– < 12 years: 38.31%), whereas RSV activity was concentrated in infants and toddlers (< 3 years: 5.30%). In older age groups, MP positivity far exceeded RSV (e.g., 6– < 12 years: 38.31% vs. 0.82%), which explains why MP appears more prevalent in the all-ages cohort. RSV remains a critical pathogen causing severe lower respiratory tract infections predominantly in young children, and its importance should not be underestimated despite the lower overall positivity rate in this study. The high susceptibility of 6– < 12 years old can be explained by aspects such as their group living characteristics, immune system development features, and social behavior traits. As semi-enclosed and high-density environments, schools provide ideal conditions for the transmission of MP through droplets. Meanwhile, since children's immune systems are not fully developed and their specific immune memory of MP is relatively limited, these factors collectively make this population the primary victims of MP infection (25).In addition, research has found that the mixed infection pattern (accounting for 17.8% of the total positive cases) provides important clues for understanding the severity of the disease. FluA + MP is the most predominant co-infection combination (accounting for 53.82% of all multiple infections), and this phenomenon deserves high-level attention. Basic research suggests that influenza virus infection can damage respiratory epithelial cells and disrupt the function of the mucosal barrier, thereby creating favorable conditions for the secondary colonization and infection of pathogens such as MP (26). Clinically, co-infection of influenza and mycoplasma may be associated with a longer fever duration, a higher risk of pulmonary imaging progression, and more complex treatment decisions (27). Our data indicate that such co-infections are more prevalent in winter, coinciding with the influenza season. This suggests that during the influenza season, for patients diagnosed with influenza, especially child patients, the possibility of MP co-infection should be vigilant to avoid missed diagnos…
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionAcute Respiratory Tract Infection (ARTI) is a leading cause of outpatient visits and emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and substantial disease burden globally. The pathogen spectrum of ARTI is complex and encompasses viruses, bacteria, and atypical pathogens (1). In China, ARTI is a prevalent infectious disease, which can lead to severe clinical consequences, especially among children, the older adult(s), and individuals with underlying diseases (2). Clarifying the epidemic characteristics of pathogens in specific periods and regions holds crucial scientific value for guiding empirical clinical treatment, implementing precise public health intervention measures (such as vaccination and seasonal prevention), and establishing effective monitoring and early warning systems.In recent years, the epidemic patterns of respiratory pathogens have changed. The global pandemic of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) that began at the end of 2019, along with the widespread implementation of Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) to contain its spread, such as wearing masks, maintaining social distancing, and restricting gatherings and travel, have profoundly altered the ecological and epidemiological characteristics of common respiratory pathogens (3). Multiple studies have confirmed that during the strict implementation of NPIs, the activity levels of many common respiratory viruses, such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), significantly decreased or even disappeared (4, 5). However, since the gradual adjustment and lifting of NPIs at the end of 2022, new trends have emerged in many parts of the world, including the resurgence of common respiratory pathogen activities, shift in epidemic seasons, and co-circulation or alternating prevalence of multiple pathogen (6). For example, post-COVID-19 pandemic surveillance in Guangdong Province revealed that the peak activity of influenza viruses has advanced, the proportion of MP infections has exceeded the pre-COVID-19 pandemic average, and there are significant age-related differences in pathogen distribution (7). These changes indicate that in the “post-COVID-19 pandemic era,” the original pathogen prevalence patterns based on historical data may no longer be applicable, and there is an urgent need for updates and analyses based on the latest monitoring data.As an important central city and transportation hub in eastern China, Hangzhou has a dense population and high population mobility, making it an ideal sentinel site for monitoring the dynamics of respiratory infectious disease. However, there is currently a lack of systematic, long-term longitudinal research covering the complete cycle before the COVID-19 pandemic, during thepandemic, and after the implementation of “Category B Management for Category B Infectious Diseases” on the epidemiological characteristics of multiple pathogens among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, especially studies that simultaneously cover viruses and atypical pathogens. To address this gap, we conducted a multicenter retrospective study of 81,974 ARTI cases from seven hospitals in Hangzhou (2018–2025) to systematically characterize the epidemiological dynamics of six common respiratory pathogens before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. 2.1.Study populationThis study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens—influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), RSV, adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP)—among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, and to evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics. A total of 81,974 patients from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou seven medical institutions in Hangzhou (see Supplementary Table 1 for details) between January 2018 and December 2025 were selected as study subjects. The diagnostic criteria for cases were as follows: pediatric cases were defined according to the Practical Pediatrics (Zhu Futang, 8th edition) (8), while adult cases were defined according to the Expert consensus on the diagnosis, treatment, and infection control of acute respiratory infections in adult outpatient and emergency departments (9), including: (1) Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI): presence of ≥2 symptoms—fever (body temperature ≥38 °C), cough, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, or sneezing—with a duration of ≤ 7 days. (2) Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI): Clinical signs: increased respiratory rate, moist rales/whistling sounds in the lungs, or tracheal retractions; Radiological evidence (X-ray/CT): signs of pneumonia/bronchitis (e.g., patchy infiltrates, atelectasis). Exclusion criteria: Incomplete clinical data, incomplete pathogen detection results, or duplicate records. Clinical data from 1,431,696 individuals undergoing respiratory pathogen screening were collected in this study. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we excluded entries with incomplete pathogen detection, removed duplicate data from repeated hospitalizations and repeated outpatient visits (1,331,565 cases), as well as duplicate data between outpatient and inpatient records (18,157 cases). Ultimately, a total of 81,974 subjects were included in the statistical analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Flowchart of the study.Flowchart illustrating a retrospective study design, showing data collection from seven medical institutions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, cohort selection process, analysis dimensions, and six key epidemiological outcomes for respiratory pathogen infections. 2.2.Data collectionDemographic and clinical data of enrolled cases were collected through the “Xiaoshan Health Data Platform” platform. The determination of infection status was based on any of the following positive test results: positive serum pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, or positive pathogen antigens or nucleic acids detected in respiratory tract samples. This study encompasses six common respiratory pathogens, including FluA, FluB, RSV, ADV, MP, and CP. For all six pathogens, specimen types included nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and blood; detection methods included serological IgM assays, antigen detection, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), with the exception that antigen detection was not included for CP. Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. Only patients with complete test results for all six target pathogens were included in the final analysis.Grouping of study subjects: in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for age-stage division and population age stratification, the study subjects were divided into six age groups: 0– < 3 years (infant and toddler group), 3– < 6 years (preschool group), 6– < 12 years (school-age group), 12– < 18 years (adolescence group), 18– < 60 years (adult group), and ≥60 years (older adult(s) group). title_original: Shifts in acute respiratory pathogen epidemiology: an 8-year surveillance study in Hangzhou, China (2018–2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens among acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI) cases in Hangzhou and evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a retrospective surveillance study conducted in Hangzhou, China, from 2018 to 2025, analyzing 81,974 patients with ARTI. Cases were tested for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP).
analysis.methods: Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. The co-infection rate was calculated, and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.
analysis.main_results: Among 81,974 patients, 33,350 tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positivity rate of 40.68%. The positivity rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022) and then rebounded sharply in the post-pandemic period (2023–2025). In contrast, RSV, ADV, and CP showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers than before the pandemic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal a dynamic shift in the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, with FluA, FluB, and MP exhibiting a "revenge rebound" after the pandemic, while RSV, ADV, and CP remained inhibited but increased in absolute numbers. This pattern highlights the complex interplay between the pandemic and seasonal respiratory pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest the need for a dynamic monitoring system to track changes in pathogen prevalence and implement targeted prevention and control measures during high-incidence seasons, particularly for FluA, FluB, and MP.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a retrospective design, which may introduce bias, and the observed changes in positivity rates could be influenced by external factors such as public health interventions. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiology of six respiratory pathogens, including seasonal influenza viruses, in Hangzhou, China, over an 8-year period from 2018 to 2025. It found that the positivity rates of influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic but rebounded sharply afterward, forming a "revenge rebound" pattern. In contrast, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP) showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers. The study highlights the need for dynamic monitoring and targeted prevention strategies during high-incidence seasons. However, the retrospective design and potential external influences limit the confidence in the findings, resulting in a moderate evidence assessment.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens among acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI) cases in Hangzhou and evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study was a retrospective surveillance study conducted in Hangzhou, China, from 2018 to 2025, analyzing 81,974 patients with ARTI. Cases were tested for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP).
analysis_en.methods: Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. The co-infection rate was calculated, and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.
analysis_en.main_results: Among 81,974 patients, 33,350 tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positivity rate of 40.68%. The positivity rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022) and then rebounded sharply in the post-pandemic period (2023–2025). In contrast, RSV, ADV, and CP showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers than before the pandemic.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal a dynamic shift in the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, with FluA, FluB, and MP exhibiting a "revenge rebound" after the pandemic, while RSV, ADV, and CP remained inhibited but increased in absolute numbers. This pattern highlights the complex interplay between the pandemic and seasonal respiratory pathogens.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest the need for a dynamic monitoring system to track changes in pathogen prevalence and implement targeted prevention and control measures during high-incidence seasons, particularly for FluA, FluB, and MP.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a retrospective design, which may introduce bias, and the observed changes in positivity rates could be influenced by external factors such as public health interventions. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses

source_records.title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses
Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses

full_text: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. MATERIALS AND METHODSCollection and purification of LCTG-001SIgA was purified and pooled from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals, as described previously (13). Briefly, frozen human milk was thawed and clarified through centrifugation and dialyzed in PBS. The supernatant was loaded onto a CaptureSelect IgA Affinity Matrix resin, and IgA was isolated as previously described (13). Pooled elution fractions were dialyzed in PBS and filtered. The final concentration was determined using a spectrophotometer.SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresisTwo micrograms of LCTG-001 was mixed with 4× lithium dodecyl sulfate loading dye and β-mercaptoethanol at 95°C for 10 min. Sample was loaded onto a 4 to 12% bis-tris gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ran at 100 V for 90 min with Bolt Mops SDS running buffer (Invitrogen). The gel was stained with Coomassie blue for 30 min at room temperature and destained using 40% methanol and 10% acetic acid in water.Neutrophil isolationNeutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood of consenting healthy male and female donors as described previously, using density gradient centrifugation (29, 30). Studies were approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board. Briefly, blood was collected into EDTA-coated tubes via venipuncture. Three milliliters of Histopaque 1119 and 3 ml of Histopaque 1077 were layered in a 15-ml Falcon tube, followed by 6 ml of blood. Samples were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 30 min at room temperature with no deceleration in an Allegra X-12R centrifuge (Beckman Coulter). The neutrophil layer was collected between the Histopaque layers and red blood cells (RBCs). Neutrophils were diluted in 50 ml of cold polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) buffer [0.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.3 mM EDTA (Invitrogen) in Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco)]. Diluted cells were centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The supernatant was discarded, the pellet was resuspended, and RBCs were lysed using ammonium-chloride-potassium (ACK) lysis buffer [NH4Cl (8.3 g/liter), KHCO3 (1 g/liter), and 0.05 mM EDTA, in sterile distilled H2O]. Cells were incubated with ACK lysis buffer for 5 min with agitation every 30 s. Following incubation, cells were diluted in 50 ml of PMN buffer and centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature, followed by an additional wash with PMN buffer. Cells were resuspended in a final volume of 1 ml in PMN buffer.Cells and virusesHuman adenocarcinoma alveolar basal epithelial (A549) cells [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)] and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (ATCC) were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells (ATCC) were maintained in Earle’s minimal essential medium (MEM Earles) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, 1% of 1 M sodium pyruvate, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Hep-2 cells (ATCC) were maintained in minimum essential medium (MEM) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Expi293 cells (Gibco) were maintained at 37°C and 8% CO2 with regular agitation (150 rpm) in Expi293 expression medium (Gibco).A/Netherlands/602/2009 H1N1 (NL/09) and X-31 (gifts from P. Palese, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, NY) were propagated in 10-day-old embryonated chicken eggs as per standard protocols (24). X-31 is a reassortant virus with the internal genes of A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1 (PR8) and the HA and NA of A/Hong Kong/1/1968 H3N2 (HK/68). A/California/04/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09) (gift from P. Palese) and A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b) (gift from Y. Berhane, CFIA, MB) were grown in MDCK cells. Cells were infected at 70% viability at a multiplicity of infection of 0.1 and incubated for 1 hour at 37°C. Following incubation, virus was removed and replaced with 1× infection media [1× MEM (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.6% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1× MEM amino acids (Gibco), 1× MEM vitamin solution (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX (Gibco), 1× penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), 0.6% sodium bicarbonate, 1× Hepes, and tolylsulfonyl phenylalanyl chloromethyl ketone (TPCK)–treated trypsin (1 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich)]. The supernatant was collected 48 hours following infection by centrifugation at 500g for 5 min. RSV A2 expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP; ViraTree) was grown in Hep-2 cells. E1/E3-deleted HuAd serotype 5 expressing GFP was a gift from Z. Xing (McMaster University, ON).H5N1 2.3.4.4b VLP productionPlasmids encoding the HA and NA from A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 were a gift from M. Côté (University of Ottawa, ON). HEK 293T cells were seeded in T150 flasks and transfected with HA and NA plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 240 μl of lipofectamine was incubated with 8 ml of Opti-MEM (Gibco) for 7.5 min. During the incubation, 32 μg of each plasmid was diluted with 8 ml of Opti-MEM. Lipofectamine and plasmid mixtures were combined and incubated at room temperature for 25 min. After the incubation, 10 ml of supplemented DMEM (2% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% GlutaMAX, and 1% Hepes) was added to the transfection mixture and incubated on cells overnight at 37°C and 5% CO2. The next day, media was replaced with DMEM containing 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX. The cell supernatant was collected 4 days posttransfection and centrifuged at 3000g for 2 min. The pellet was removed, and the supernatant was stored at −80°C.Transmission electron microscopyA 3-μl drop of sample was applied to a formvar-coated copper grid stabilized with a 5-nm carbon film and left for 10 min to allow for the VLPs to settle on the grid. Excess sample was blotted off with filter paper. The grids were then briefly rinsed by immersion in deionized water and blotted dry with filter paper. Then, 3 μl of 1% (aq) uranyl acetate was applied to the grid surface and left for 1 min. Excess stain was removed by blotting with filter paper, and the grid was allowed to dry completely. Imaging of the grids was performed using a TALOS L120C transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. Images were acquired with a 4K CETA complementary metal-oxide semiconductor camera.Influenza A virus purificationClarified supernatants from IAV-infected MDCK cells or allantoic fluid from embryonated chicken eggs were layered on top of 8 ml of 20% sucrose in NTE [0.5 M NaCl, 10 mM tris HCl, and 1 mM EDTA (pH 7.5)] buffer in Ultra-Clear Ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 2 hours at 4°C at 76650g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 4 hours at 4°C at 135,000g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

full_text_sections.results: RESULTSAssessment of broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogensUnlike IgG in conventional IVIG or convalescent plasma, which is peripherally sourced from the circulation, SIgA is exclusively found at mucosal sites. Sourcing from the respiratory mucosa is not feasible due to procedural complexities and limited antibody yield. To circumvent these limitations, we explored breast milk as an alternative source of mucosal SIgA. Breast milk is a scalable and sustainable source of mucosal SIgA, and donations of extra breast milk are already collected by over 700 human milk banks worldwide. To produce purified SIgA, breast milk samples were collected from 120 lactating donors through collaborations with milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Initial sample shipments included 85 donor contributions received on 11 October 2022, followed by an additional 35 samples on 29 November 2022. The samples, collected throughout 2022, were pooled to yield a total volume of 15,585 ml. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. The purity of LCTG-001 was confirmed by Coomassie staining (fig. S1) and was consistent with previous reports (13). The donor cohort was not screened for recent infection or vaccination status, thereby aligning with conventional IVIG collection practices in which donors are not selected on the basis of prior antigenic exposures (3, 14).We next evaluated whether the polyclonal SIgA pool, LCTG-001, could recognize and neutralize a panel of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus (HuAd), and IAV. Representative strains and serotypes were selected for each virus to assess LCTG-001’s binding and neutralizing potency. To assess LCTG-001’s antiviral activity, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to evaluate antibody binding, alongside microneutralization (MNT) assays to measure functional neutralization.We first assessed binding of LCTG-001 to RSV fusion protein (RSV-F), the antigen used in licensed RSV vaccines (15). LCTG-001 demonstrated robust binding to RSV-F (AUC = 62.02 ± 1.273; Fig. 1A), and these antibodies were able to neutralize RSV at physiologically relevant concentrations [median inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 320 μg/ml; Fig. 1B].Fig. 1.LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogens.(A, C, and E) LCTG-001 binding responses to RSV-F (A), HuAd5 lysate (C), and Cal/09 HA (E). (B, D, and F) LCTG-001 neutralizing antibody responses to RSV (B), HuAd5 (D), and Cal/09 (F), measured by percent (%) neutralization using MNT assays. Data presented in (A) to (F) represent mean ± SEM. Data presented in (A), (C), and (E) represent three technical replicates. Data presented in (B), (D), and (F) are from three independent experiments.We next assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against adenovirus, focusing on HuAd type 5 (HuAd5), one of the most prevalent HuAd serotypes (16, 17). ELISAs were performed using the lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells as a source of antigen (18). Again, LCTG-001 demonstrated specific binding to the lysate of infected cells (AUC = 62.28 ± 2.309; Fig. 1C) and neutralized HuAd5 with considerable potency (IC50 = 180 μg/ml; Fig. 1D).Last, we assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against IAV. IAV is a respiratory virus responsible for both seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics, with five pandemics in the last century (19). We first investigated the ability of LCTG-001 to recognize and neutralize A/California/07/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09). Cal/09 (H1N1) is an isolate from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which then circulated seasonally and was a recommended seasonal influenza vaccine strain for more than 5 years in North America. Hence, most of the population has been exposed through infection and/or vaccination. Similar to RSV and HuAd5, LCTG-001 showed specific binding to Cal/09 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA) (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E) and neutralization activity (IC50 = 670 μg/ml; Fig. 1F). Together, these findings demonstrate that LCTG-001, a breast milk–derived polyclonal SIgA product, exhibits broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple clinically relevant respiratory pathogens.LCTG-001 engages nonneutralizing antibody effector functions against H1N1 IAVWhile vaccination remains the primary strategy for control of seasonal influenza, antigenic drift, particularly in the HA head domain, limits vaccine effectiveness and necessitates regular vaccine strain updates. Antibody responses generated by infection or vaccination primarily target the immunodominant HA head, which can significantly vary between strains. Unlike the variable HA head, the stalk domain is relatively conserved, with stalk-specific antibodies capable of providing protection against diverse IAV strains (20). However, stalk-specific antibody responses are typically low in magnitude but tend to increase with age and influenza virus exposures (21, 22). Despite this, these antibodies can provide broad protection by targeting conserved stalk epitopes, particularly in the context of vaccine mismatch or exposure to novel pandemic strains where HA head-specific immunity is lacking. Hence, we next sought to determine whether stalk-specific anti-IAV antibodies were present in LCTG-001 through the use of a chimeric HA protein (cH6/1) composed of the conserved stalk domain of A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) and the head domain from the avian A/mallard/Sweden/81/02 (H6N2) strain (23). The use of an avian H6 head, which is rarely encountered in humans, allows for measurement of stalk-specific binding antibodies (24). Using this approach, LCTG-001 demonstrated stalk-specific binding antibody responses (AUC = 46.35 ± 9.036; Fig. 2A) that were not statistically different (P = 0.54) from antibody responses to full-length Cal/09 (H1N1) HA (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E), suggesting that a large proportion of H1 HA-specific antibodies present in LCTG-001 recognizes the H1 stalk. These data indicate that LCTG-001 contains stalk-binding antibodies against IAV.Fig. 2.LCTG-001 engages nonneutralizing antibody effector functions against H1N1 IAV.(A) LCTG-001 binding responses to cH6/1 HA. (B) Anti–neuraminidase (NA) activity of LCTG-001 against Cal/09 (H1N1), measured by percent (%) inhibition with an enzyme-linked lectin assay (ELLA). (C) Primary human neutrophils were isolated and assessed for their ability to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) in an in vitro luminol-based assay with LCTG-001 and Cal/09 (H1N1). ROS production was measured using relative light units (RLU). Data presented in (A) represent mean ± SEM of three technical replicates. Data presented in (B) represent mean ± SEM of three technical replicates. Data presented in (C) are a representative time course data for a single experiment with three technical replicates with mean ± SEM.Antibodies that bind near the enzymatic site of neuraminidase (NA) exert antiviral activity by inhibiting NA function (25). In addition, previous reports indicate that stalk-specific antibodies can prevent or interfere with viral infection through a variety of mechanisms, including NA inhibition (26). Antibodies that bind to the HA stalk can interfere with NA activity through steric hindrance (27). Therefore, we next assessed whether the antibodies present in LCTG-001 could inhibit the enzymatic activity of NA. An enzyme-linked lectin assay (ELLA) was performed to measure inhibition of NA-mediated cleavage of terminal sialic acids from fetuin, a sialylated glycoprotein substrate (28). LCTG-001 potently inhibited the NA activity of Cal/09 (H1N1) (IC50 = 8.7 μg; Fig. 2B).Stalk-binding antibodies also induce Fc-dependent effector functions, including through Fc receptor engagement on the surface of immune cells. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONIn this study, we evaluated the antiviral activity and protective efficacy of LCTG-001, a polyclonal SIgA product derived from pooled human breast milk, as a novel mucosal passive immunization strategy that can address the inherent limitations associated with conventional intravenous, IgG-based treatments. IVIG and monoclonal antibody passive immunization strategies, while standard of care in the field for conferring prophylactic and/or therapeutic protection against respiratory pathogens, often have limited transudation to the respiratory mucosa (36–39). These therapies are also logistically burdensome due to the need for parenteral administration in health care settings and are associated with a variety of side effects, including infusion-related reactions (40).In contrast to the periphery, the predominant antibody isotype found in the respiratory mucosa is SIgA. SIgA is actively transported across epithelial barriers and is highly resistant to proteolytic degradation, making it well suited for conferring protection within the respiratory mucosa (41). Moreover, SIgA is naturally localized to mucosa through polymeric immunoglobulin receptor–mediated epithelial transport, depositing IgA into the lumen where respiratory viruses establish infection, a targeted delivery that serum-derived IgG achieves only sparingly (11, 39, 41, 42).Our results demonstrate that LCTG-001 has broad-spectrum antiviral activity mediated by multiple mechanisms. This polyclonal SIgA neutralized diverse respiratory viruses, including RSV, adenovirus, and representatives of both circulating human group 1 and group 2 IAV subtypes, including those with pandemic potential, thereby highlighting its exceptionally broad reactivity. Similarly, polyclonal SIgA compositions administered via the intranasal and intratracheal route were able to neutralize SARS-CoV-2 in K18+ hACE2 transgenic mice (13). This breadth of activity likely arises from the rich and diverse pool of SIgA isolated from pooled breast milk, capturing a wide array of antibodies with varying specificities within a single product.Notably, LCTG-001 not only inhibited IAV viral entry in vitro but also exhibited robust NA inhibition. While NA antibodies may not be potently neutralizing, they can limit viral spread and have been shown to correlate with protection in influenza infection (43–45). Both HA stalk binding and NA-specific antibodies can contribute to NAI activity, the former through steric hindrance of the NA binding site and the latter by directly binding near the enzymatic site of the protein (26, 27). The presence of NAI activity suggests that LCTG-001 can impair virion release, even in the context of strains for which conventional neutralizing antibodies are absent. Furthermore, LCTG-001 induced Fc-dependent activation of neutrophils, as evidenced by a luminol-based assay. In humans, IgA is known to engage FcαRI (CD89) on myeloid cells, triggering processes like phagocytosis, respiratory burst, and NETosis (29, 30). Our data confirm that a complex SIgA pool from breast milk can harness this pathway. Thus, beyond classical neutralization, LCTG-001 is capable of activating innate immune cells to facilitate pathogen clearance. The ability of SIgA to activate neutrophils has important implications for mucosal defense. IgA is often viewed as a non-inflammatory “shield” that blocks pathogen entry. Here, we show that SIgA can also engage innate immunity, further facilitating pathogen clearance. This FcαRI-dependent mechanism adds a crucial layer of protection at mucosal surfaces.Our use of a polyclonal human SIgA pool from breast milk reveals the breadth of Fc-mediated activity of LCTG-001 in the context of IAV. Prior studies have mostly examined serum-derived or engineered monomeric IgA (29, 30, 46). SIgA can engage the FcαR on cells; however, this interaction requires accessory molecules such as MAC-1 and results in a lower affinity compared to cross-linked monomeric IgA (47–49). Hence, the ability of SIgA to engage Fc-mediated neutrophil effector functions in an IAV antigen–specific context has not been fully examined. We demonstrated that the polyclonal SIgA which comprises LCTG-001 retains the ability to engage Fc effector functions on neutrophils, triggering a potent effector response against three different strains of IAV. This novel finding further broadens the paradigm of how SIgA contributes to antiviral immunity, indicating that SIgA-based interventions could actively modulate the innate immune milieu in the airways during respiratory viral infection.Another notable aspect of LCTG-001’s efficacy is its breadth of antiviral activities against IAVs. Our data suggest that this polyclonal mixture appears to target multiple viral proteins and life cycle steps: We detected antibodies likely directed against the conserved HA stalk, those capable of inhibiting NA (mediating NAI), and antibodies capable of stimulating Fc-dependent effector functions. These modes of action are complementary, and the interplay between Fab-mediated and Fc-mediated functions is evident in our data. In essence, LCTG-001 may not rely on a single mechanism of action but rather uses a variety of effector functions to mediate protection against viral pathogens. This was evident after H1N1 challenge, where there was incomplete neutralization at the highest concentration of antibody tested. Despite this, we observed high binding activity to Cal/09 (H1N1) HA. full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONImmunoglobulin replacement therapy, which can take the form of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or subcutaneous immunoglobulin, is essential for mitigating infectious diseases and is especially critical in treating primary immunodeficiencies such as common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID is characterized by impaired antibody production, manifesting as reduced levels of immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgA, and/or IgM (1, 2). Regular IVIG infusions are administered to patients with CVID to replenish immunoglobulin levels, thereby reducing infection frequency and severity (3). Despite its effectiveness, IVIG therapy is costly, invasive, and requires frequent medically assisted administration (1, 4).Beyond management of immunoglobulin immunodeficiencies, IVIG and convalescent plasma have also been used as passive immunization strategies to protect populations against viral infections, including in pandemic settings where vaccines are either unavailable or in limited supply. This was exemplified during the 1918 and 2009 influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics, as well as during the initial stages of COVID-19 (5–8). However, these strategies require intravenous administration of antibodies derived from the circulation, which are rich in IgG and monomeric IgA but differ markedly from the predominantly dimeric and secretory IgA (SIgA) present at mucosal surfaces (9). Thus, these approaches do not fully recapitulate the protective immune landscape of the respiratory mucosa found in healthy individuals (4, 10). In addition, antibodies administered intravenously must transudate from the circulation to the mucosal surfaces to exert their protective effects, which limits availability at respiratory surfaces (11). This limitation highlights the need for mucosally delivered passive immunization strategies which can deliver antibodies directly to the site of pathogen entry.Sourcing SIgA from human biospecimens, such as those found in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluids, is not practical due to the invasiveness of the procedures and the limited yield of antibodies. In contrast, breast milk is a more attractive source that is more plentiful, accessible, and rich in mucosal SIgA (12). Previous work has demonstrated that breast milk–derived SIgA has antiviral activity against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and is a viable prophylactic strategy in preclinical models (13). This study used breast milk from human milk donors post–SARS-CoV-2 infection, thereby enriching the antibody pool for anti–SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. Building on these observations, we hypothesized that purifying IgA from a large sample of donors without screening milk samples for neutralizing antibodies against any particular pathogen would yield a polyclonal SIgA product with broad antiviral activity against a diverse array of respiratory pathogens due to varied donor exposures to infections and/or vaccinations, akin to IVIG.Here, we investigate a polyclonal, breast milk–derived SIgA product, LCTG-001. Our findings demonstrate that LCTG-001 exhibits broad antiviral activity in vitro against a panel of respiratory pathogens. We further demonstrate that LCTG-001 has neutralizing and nonneutralizing activity against both group 1 and group 2 IAVs, in addition to activity against emerging zoonotic strains. Last, we demonstrate that when delivered directly to the respiratory mucosa, LCTG-001 was protective in vivo against IAV challenge in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. Collectively, these results highlight mucosal delivery of breast milk–derived IgA as a passive immunization strategy capable of addressing limitations inherent in traditional intravenous antibody therapies, offering potential protection against both endemic and pandemic respiratory infections. Assessment of broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogensUnlike IgG in conventional IVIG or convalescent plasma, which is peripherally sourced from the circulation, SIgA is exclusively found at mucosal sites. Sourcing from the respiratory mucosa is not feasible due to procedural complexities and limited antibody yield. To circumvent these limitations, we explored breast milk as an alternative source of mucosal SIgA. Breast milk is a scalable and sustainable source of mucosal SIgA, and donations of extra breast milk are already collected by over 700 human milk banks worldwide. To produce purified SIgA, breast milk samples were collected from 120 lactating donors through collaborations with milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Initial sample shipments included 85 donor contributions received on 11 October 2022, followed by an additional 35 samples on 29 November 2022. The samples, collected throughout 2022, were pooled to yield a total volume of 15,585 ml. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. The purity of LCTG-001 was confirmed by Coomassie staining (fig. S1) and was consistent with previous reports (13). The donor cohort was not screened for recent infection or vaccination status, thereby aligning with conventional IVIG collection practices in which donors are not selected on the basis of prior antigenic exposures (3, 14).We next evaluated whether the polyclonal SIgA pool, LCTG-001, could recognize and neutralize a panel of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus (HuAd), and IAV. Representative strains and serotypes were selected for each virus to assess LCTG-001’s binding and neutralizing potency. To assess LCTG-001’s antiviral activity, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to evaluate antibody binding, alongside microneutralization (MNT) assays to measure functional neutralization.We first assessed binding of LCTG-001 to RSV fusion protein (RSV-F), the antigen used in licensed RSV vaccines (15). LCTG-001 demonstrated robust binding to RSV-F (AUC = 62.02 ± 1.273; Fig. 1A), and these antibodies were able to neutralize RSV at physiologically relevant concentrations [median inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 320 μg/ml; Fig. 1B].Fig. 1.LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogens.(A, C, and E) LCTG-001 binding responses to RSV-F (A), HuAd5 lysate (C), and Cal/09 HA (E). (B, D, and F) LCTG-001 neutralizing antibody responses to RSV (B), HuAd5 (D), and Cal/09 (F), measured by percent (%) neutralization using MNT assays. Data presented in (A) to (F) represent mean ± SEM. Data presented in (A), (C), and (E) represent three technical replicates. Data presented in (B), (D), and (F) are from three independent experiments.We next assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against adenovirus, focusing on HuAd type 5 (HuAd5), one of the most prevalent HuAd serotypes (16, 17). ELISAs were performed using the lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells as a source of antigen (18). Again, LCTG-001 demonstrated specific binding to the lysate of infected cells (AUC = 62.28 ± 2.309; Fig. 1C) and neutralized HuAd5 with considerable potency (IC50 = 180 μg/ml; Fig. 1D).Last, we assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against IAV. IAV is a respiratory virus responsible for both seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics, with five pandemics in the last century (19). We first investigated the ability of LCTG-001 to recognize and neutralize A/California/07/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09). Cal/09 (H1N1) is an isolate from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which then circulated seasonally and was a recommended seasonal influenza vaccine strain for more than 5 years in North America. Hence, most of the population has been exposed through infection and/or vaccination. Similar to RSV and HuAd5, LCTG-001 showed specific binding to Cal/09 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA) (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E) and neutralization activity (IC50 = 670 μg/ml; Fig. 1F). full_text_excerpt: These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address limitations in current antiviral protection methods by testing LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from human breast milk, against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including influenza A virus, to provide broad antiviral protection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the collection and purification of LCTG-001 from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals and testing it against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus in cell cultures and neutrophils.
analysis.methods: LCTG-001 was purified and tested for antiviral activity using cell cultures and neutrophils. The methods included SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, density gradient centrifugation, and transmission electron microscopy for virus purification and quantification.
analysis.main_results: LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as novel evidence of broad antiviral protection provided by LCTG-001, which could be useful for preventing multiple respiratory viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new antiviral strategies for preventing respiratory infections, particularly in vulnerable populations such as infants and the elderly.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of in vitro models and the need for further clinical validation. The evidence strength is moderate due to the in vitro nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation from human breast milk, against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus, demonstrating broad antiviral activity. The findings suggest potential for new antiviral strategies but require further clinical validation.

full_text: AbstractInfectious diseases in domestic animals—including those with zoonotic potential—impose a substantial global burden on food security, livelihoods, and public health. Environmental surveillance (ES) offers a critical complement to conventional animal-level diagnostics by detecting pathogens or their genetic signatures directly in the matrices through which they persist and spread: water, soil, air, manure, fomites, and arthropod vectors. This review synthesizes evidence across three analytical dimensions—matrix suitability, detection method performance, and wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE)—for 15 viral, bacterial, and parasitological diseases of domestic animals. Key findings reveal that matrix choice profoundly governs detection sensitivity: surface water and wetland sediments support infectious avian influenza virus isolation; pooled environmental feces and slurry outperform individual animal sampling for Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP); and electrostatic dust cloths enable simultaneous detection of peste-des-petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and capripoxviruses at livestock markets. Molecular methods, principally quantitative RT-PCR and droplet digital PCR, consistently outperform conventional culture in sensitivity and turnaround time, though viability-linked assays remain an important unresolved need. WBE is increasingly applied beyond human pathogens: piggery effluent surveillance for Japanese encephalitis virus and wastewater metagenomics for antimicrobial resistance exemplify its veterinary potential. Interpretive limitations persist, including matrix-driven inhibition, absence of harmonized protocols, and the challenge of equating nucleic-acid signals with infectious risk. Realizing the full promise of ES within a One Health framework requires standardized, field-validated sampling workflows, viability-linked molecular assays, and formal integration of environmental signals into routine veterinary surveillance and outbreak-response systems.Keywords: animal disease surveillance, environmental surveillance, molecular detection, non-invasive surveillance, One Health, wastewater-based epidemiology 2.Methodologies of environmental surveillanceThe efficacy of ES hinges on the appropriate selection and application of various methodologies for sample collection, pathogen detection, and data analysis.2.1.Sample collectionEnvironmental samples can be diverse, reflecting the various routes of pathogen shedding and persistence in the environment. Common sample types include:Water and effluent samples: Collected from drinking troughs, surface waters, drainage run-off, lagoons, and municipal/on-farm effluent streams to detect waterborne viruses and enteric bacteria (5). Operational protocols typically require 500 mL to 5 L volumes for surface waters (concentrated via dead-end ultrafiltration or electronegative membrane adsorption) and 100 mL to 1 L for high-turbidity slurry or wastewater effluents (processed via skimmed-milk flocculation or centrifugal ultrafiltration). 24-h composite sampling is recommended for effluent streams to account for diurnal shedding variations, accompanied by trip and field blank quality controls.Air samples: Collected using liquid impingers, solid impactors, or cyclone air samplers to detect aerosolized respiratory pathogens in confined animal housing, live bird markets, and farm perimeters ((8, 9)). Standardized protocols employ personal or stationary liquid impingers (e.g., operating at 12.5 L/min for 30–60 min into collection fluids supplemented with viral transport medium and protein stabilizers) or high-volume dry cyclone samplers (50–100 L/min for 1–2 h). Field air blanks and meteorological records (relative humidity, temperature, airflow velocity) are mandatory for quantitative comparability.Soil and bedding samples: Relevant for environmentally robust pathogens such as bacterial spores (Bacillus anthracis), mycobacteria, and protozoan oocysts that persist in soil microhabitats or barn bedding (10). Protocols necessitate core sampling across multiple high-traffic points (minimum 5–10 sub-samples per pen or pasture sector, pooled to 100–250 g), with immediate transport at 4 °C, desiccation prevention, and mechanical bead-beating cell disruption to overcome soil particle adsorption.Fomite and surface samples: Swabs from surfaces, equipment, vehicles, animal crates, or footwear that facilitate indirect transmission (11). Standardized protocols use pre-moistened macrofoam or synthetic swabs (wetted with buffered peptone water, PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20, or viral transport medium) rubbed across defined surface areas (100–500 cm2 per surface). For large-area poultry floor monitoring, paired boot-sock swabs walked over a minimum of 100 m traverse provide operationally validated flock-level sensitivity.Manure and slurry samples: Pooled composite samples from animal waste channels, slurry pits, or manure heaps offering aggregated herd-level shedding signals (12). Representative protocols require 10–20 sub-aliquots collected across dung channels or holding lagoons (total 50–100 g composite), followed by thorough homogenization, enzymatic/mechanical lysis, and the incorporation of internal amplification controls to detect potent PCR inhibitors (bile salts, polyphenols, and humic compounds).Dust samples: Accumulations of settled or airborne dust in livestock facilities contain desiccation-resistant pathogen nucleic acids, providing a cumulative measure of shedding over days to weeks (7). Standardized electrostatic dust wipes (20 × 20 cm cloths sampled over 1–5 m2 horizontal surfaces) or passive settling plates deployed for 7–14 days allow low-cost, non-invasive herd-level surveillance at animal aggregation points and live markets.The selection of sample type is influenced by the pathogen’s epidemiological traits, its ability to persist in various environments, and the goals of the surveillance effort. For instance, air sampling is typically most effective for respiratory pathogens, while manure or wastewater is often more appropriate for enteric pathogens that are excreted at the group level.Ensuring proper sample preservation and transport is crucial for accurate interpretation. Handling procedures specific to the matrix, such as maintaining temperature control (cold chain at 4 °C for immediate processing or −80 °C for biobanking), rapid transport, the addition of antimicrobial/antifungal cocktails to culture media, and the prevention of repeated freeze–thaw cycles, must be strictly enforced. Comprehensive quality assurance requires the routine inclusion of field trip blanks (to monitor collection and transport contamination), negative extraction controls, matrix-matched positive spikes (to calculate recovery efficiency), and exogenous internal amplification controls (IACs, such as bacteriophage MS2, equine arteritis virus, or phocid herpesvirus-1) spiked into every PCR reaction to detect false-negative results caused by environmental matrix inhibitors.2.2.Pathogen detection methodsOnce samples are collected, various laboratory techniques are employed for pathogen detection:Molecular Methods:Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and quantitative PCR (qPCR): Widely used for rapid and sensitive detection of pathogen nucleic acids (DNA/RNA). qPCR provides quantitative data on pathogen load (13).Next,-Generation Sequencing (NGS) / Metagenomics: Offers broad-spectrum detection of known and unknown pathogens, enabling strain typing, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, and understanding of microbial communities (4).Loop-mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP): A simpler, rapid, and often field-deployable molecular technique for pathogen detection (14).Culture-based methods: involve traditional microbiological approaches for isolating and identifying living pathogens. Although these methods are slower, they confirm the pathogens’ viability and enable further analysis, such as testing for antimicrobial susceptibility.Antigen Detection Assays: Less common for environmental samples but can be used for specific pathogens where robust antibody-based detection is feasible (15).Biosensors: are becoming valuable additions to traditional lab techniques due to their ability to facilitate quick and portable detection directly in the field. These instruments integrate a biological recognition component, such as an antibody, enzyme, or nucleic-acid probe, with a transducer that translates the biological interaction into a quantifiable electrical, optical, or thermal signal (16). Their advantage lies in their speed and suitability for field use, although it is still essential to validate their analytical performance across complex environmental matrices.When evaluating detection methods, it is crucial to consider factors such as matrix effects, recovery efficiency, analytical sensitivity, specificity, and the difference between identifying nucleic acid and proving the presence of a viable pathogen. Quality control necessitates the use of field blanks, extraction and amplification controls, conducting tests in duplicates when possible, and clearly reporting detection limits. In practice, the selection of a method is also influenced by factors like cost, turnaround time, available infrastructure, and whether the goal of surveillance is rapid screening, confirmatory diagnosis, strain characterization, or ongoing monitoring. The relative performance of these techniques across different environmental matrices, and their practical trade-offs under field conditions, are summarized in Table 1 and revisited in the context of specific disease applications in Section 3 (Figure 2).Table 1Comparative overview of environmental pathogen detection methods. Its foundational logic is straightforward: infected individuals—whether human or animal—shed pathogens or their nucleic acids in feces, urine, and respiratory secretions, which enter wastewater streams and can be detected before clinical case counts reflect true transmission intensity. During the COVID-19 pandemic, WBE demonstrated a capacity to anticipate clinical surges by 7–14 days in urban catchments (4, 5), establishing a blueprint now being adapted to veterinary and One Health applications.In domestic animal contexts, the most compelling application of WBE to date involves on-farm effluent surveillance for Japanese encephalitis virus. Ahmed et al. (3) demonstrated that JEV RNA is consistently detectable in piggery effluent during active transmission seasons, offering a herd-level signal that bypasses the logistical complexity of individual pig sampling in large intensive operations. The complementarity with mosquito-trap surveillance is striking: while vector trapping captures transmission pressure in the broader environment, piggery WBE reflects viral amplification within the key vertebrate amplifier host, potentially enabling earlier intervention. Similarly, municipal wastewater surveillance detected JEV RNA during an acute disease outbreak in Australia, underscoring the broader catchment-level sensitivity of this approach (3). A concrete operational blueprint for veterinary WBE is provided by wastewater monitoring for JEV in intensive pig production catchments. In this integrated surveillance framework: (1) routine weekly effluent composite samples are collected from piggery drainage channels and effluent ponds; (2) rapid RT-qPCR screening quantifies JEV RNA load relative to an endogenous control; (3) crossing an actionable threshold (e.g., progressive cycle threshold decline or >10^3 viral genome copies/L) immediately triggers a multi-agency tiered response: (a) targeted vector surveillance intensification by deploying CO2-baited light traps within a 3–5 km buffer zone to determine Culex tritaeniorhynchus / Culex annulirostris abundance and vector infection rates; (b) immediate vector abatement through larvicide application in effluent ponds and surrounding breeding waters, accompanied by barrier thermal fogging with adulticides; (c) herd health interventions, including piggery movement standstill orders, vector screening of breeding stock, and booster vaccination where authorized; and (d) public health notifications to local health authorities to issue mosquito avoidance advisories, enforce personal protective equipment for farm personnel, and prioritize human JEV vaccination in surrounding communities. This operational continuum exemplifies how environmental pathogen detection in animal waste streams directly informs upstream vector control and prevents downstream zoonotic spillover.Beyond specific viral targets, metagenomic WBE offers unbiased pathogen and antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) surveillance without a priori target selection. Brumfield et al. (4) demonstrated that metatranscriptomic sequencing of wastewater captures not only SARS-CoV-2 but co-circulating bacterial and parasitic agents, viral diversity indices, and ARG profiles—collectively providing a rich epidemiological landscape. For veterinary surveillance, this is particularly relevant to intensive livestock production systems, where dense animal housing, prophylactic antimicrobial use, and high fecal biomass create wastewater streams rich in both pathogens and resistance determinants. (12) identified a broad array of potential bacterial pathogens and ARGs in soil floors and cow dung from rural Bangladesh households, reinforcing the value of environmental fecal matrices as resistance surveillance substrates.Seasonal dynamics in WBE are a further analytical asset. (5) revealed distinct seasonal signatures for respiratory, enteric, and urinary viruses across a year-long wastewater sequencing program, demonstrating that metagenomics can track viral community composition shifts that precede clinical outbreak detection. Adapting this framework to livestock wastewater—where seasonal stocking densities, climate conditions, and disease calendars create predictable shedding windows—represents a high-priority research avenue. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionEnvironmental surveillance has matured from a research curiosity into an operationally relevant pillar of infectious disease monitoring in domestic animal populations, and the evidence reviewed here demonstrates its distinctive and irreplaceable epidemiological contributions. Across 15 disease contexts—from FMDV aerosol persistence in endemic settings to eDNA detection of Fasciola metacercariae on pasture; from WBE for JEV in piggery effluent to molecular bTB detection at wildlife-cattle interfaces—ES has consistently demonstrated the capacity to detect transmission before clinical cases accumulate, to characterize contamination hotspots with spatial granularity impossible through animal-level surveillance alone, and to integrate across human, animal, and environmental health data streams in the spirit of the One Health framework.Matrix selection remains the foundational decision in ES design, and our comparative analysis across diseases reveals consistent patterns: water bodies and aquatic sediments are optimal for AIV, Leptospira, and JEV; pooled environmental faeces and litter excel for MAP, Salmonella, Eimeria, and enteric viruses; air sampling adds unique detection windows for respiratory pathogens including HPAI and NDV; tick-based environmental sampling is indispensable for babesiosis and theileriosis; and fomite and dust cloth swabbing provides cost-effective, simultaneous multi-pathogen signals at livestock markets and household interfaces.Realizing the full promise of ES within routine veterinary surveillance requires progress on four interconnected fronts: (i) harmonized, matrix-validated standard operating procedures that enable inter-laboratory and cross-national comparability; (ii) viability-linked molecular assays that distinguish infectious risk from nucleic acid residue; (iii) evidence-based decision thresholds that translate environmental signals into defined management actions; and (iv) data integration infrastructure that connects ES outputs to national veterinary reporting systems, outbreak investigation databases, and risk-based surveillance programs. Wastewater-based epidemiology, which has demonstrated dramatic utility in human health surveillance, is an underexploited frontier in veterinary ES that deserves structured research investment, particularly for intensively-reared species and zoonotic pathogens where population-level monitoring without animal handling is a practical imperative. With these foundations in place, ES is poised to transition from an investigational adjunct into a routine surveillance modality that, in concert with animal-level and genomic surveillance, forms the sensing infrastructure for a genuinely integrated One Health disease intelligence system.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionEnvironmental surveillance (ES) is an increasingly indispensable component of infectious disease monitoring in domestic animal populations. Rather than relying exclusively on clinical presentation or individual animal testing—approaches that are inherently reactive and epidemiologically incomplete—ES interrogates the matrices through which pathogens are shed, persist, and transmitted. By doing so, it can detect pathogen circulation ahead of clinical case accrual, characterize transmission hotspots, and generate population-level risk signals that individual animal-based surveillance structurally cannot. This capacity is particularly valuable under field conditions where direct sampling is logistically constrained—migratory bird flocks, wild boar populations, informal livestock markets, and free-ranging ruminants all present practical barriers to representative animal-level sampling that ES can partially circumvent.In practice, ES encompasses the systematic collection and analysis of water, air, soil, bedding, manure, fomites, arthropod vectors, and other environmental matrices from farms, markets, water bodies, and shared wildlife–livestock interfaces (1, 2). These samples can reveal pathogen presence, environmental persistence half-lives, genetic diversity, and shedding dynamics—information that collectively sharpens our understanding of source attribution and transmission route characterization. The advent of environmental DNA (eDNA) and environmental RNA (eRNA) methodologies, combined with quantitative PCR (qPCR), droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), and metagenomic sequencing, has dramatically extended the analytical sensitivity and breadth of ES, enabling detection of pathogens at concentrations that culture-based and antigen detection approaches routinely fail to capture.Expanding the ES framework substantially, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) utilizes municipal and on-farm wastewater as aggregated, non-invasive sentinels for pathogen circulation at population scale (Figure 1). Originally pioneered for poliovirus and accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic, WBE is now demonstrating veterinary relevance. For example, piggery effluent surveillance has successfully detected Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) RNA during active outbreaks (3). Furthermore, metagenomic WBE can profile antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) reservoirs across entire livestock production catchments (4, 5). Complementarily, remote sensing and geospatial analysis—mapping vector breeding habitats, wetland connectivity, and wildlife movement corridors—provide ecological context that transforms discrete environmental detections into spatially coherent risk maps (6, 7). To systematically evaluate the state of knowledge and operational utility of ES, this review synthesizes evidence across 15 major infectious diseases of domestic livestock and poultry, categorized into three etiologic groups: (1) viral diseases (n = 7): Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), Peste des petits ruminants (PPR), Lumpy skin disease (LSD), Avian influenza (AI), Newcastle disease (ND), African swine fever (ASF), and Japanese encephalitis (JE); (2) bacterial diseases (n = 4): Salmonellosis (Salmonella enterica), Paratuberculosis / Johne’s disease (Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis, MAP), Leptospirosis (pathogenic Leptospira spp.), and Bovine tuberculosis (Mycobacterium bovis, bTB); and (3) parasitological diseases (n = 4): Coccidiosis (Eimeria spp.), Fasciolosis (Fasciola hepatica and F. gigantica), Babesiosis (Babesia spp.), and Theileriosis (Theileria spp.). This review synthesizes these dimensions across 15 diseases of domestic animals, evaluating ES through three analytical lenses: (i) matrix suitability and pathogen survival, (ii) detection method performance under field conditions, and (iii) the emerging contribution of WBE and non-invasive sampling. Key findings reveal that matrix choice profoundly governs detection sensitivity: surface water and wetland sediments support infectious avian influenza virus isolation; pooled environmental feces and slurry outperform individual animal sampling for Mycobacterium avium subsp. Molecular methods, principally quantitative RT-PCR and droplet digital PCR, consistently outperform conventional culture in sensitivity and turnaround time, though viability-linked assays remain an important unresolved need.
